# Nilpotent orbits of orthogonal groups over $p$ -adic fields, and the DeBacker parametrizationThanks: 1 This author’s research is supported by a Discovery Grant from NSERC Canada.Thanks: 2 Corresponding author.

**Authors:** Tobias Bernstein Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Canada Email address: tobias.toby.bernstein@gmail.com , Jia-Jun Ma Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 800 Dongchuan Rd Shanghai, 200240, China Email address: hoxide@sjtu.edu.cn , Monica Nevins1,2 Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Canada Email address: mnevins@uottawa.ca and Jit Wu Yap Address: Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, Block S17, 10 Lower Kent Ridge Road, Singapore 119076 Email address: yapjitwu@gmail.com

## Abstract

For local non-archimedean fields $k$ of sufficiently large residual characteristic, we explicitly parametrize and count the rational nilpotent adjoint orbits in each algebraic orbit of orthogonal and special orthogonal groups. We separately give an explicit algorithmic construction for representatives of each orbit. We then, in the general setting of groups $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(D)$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{n}(D)$ (where $D$ is a central division algebra over $k$ ) or classical groups, give a new characterisation of the “building set” (defined by DeBacker) of an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -triple in terms of the building of its centralizer. Using this, we prove our construction realizes DeBacker’s parametrization of rational nilpotent orbits via elements of the Bruhat-Tits building.

#### Key words and phrases:

#### 1991 Mathematics Subject Classification

## 1. Introduction

Rational, or arithmetic, nilpotent adjoint orbits of algebraic groups over a local field $k$ arise in representation theory in several contexts. For example, the Harish-Chandra–Howe character formula locally expresses a character of a representation as a linear combination of (Fourier transforms of) nilpotent orbital integrals. As another example, the orbit method would parametrize representations by admissible coadjoint orbits, with the admissible nilpotent orbits corresponding to core singular cases.

Algebraic, or geometric, nilpotent adjoint orbits can be thought of as those under the algebraic group over the algebraic closure of the local field. These orbits can be parameterized in multiple ways, including the Bala-Carter classification (extended to low characteristic by McNinch and others), weighted Dynkin diagrams, and partition-type classifications (for classical groups).

The rational points of an algebraic orbit form zero or more rational orbits, and these can in principle be counted using Galois cohomology; yet it remained an open combinatorial problem to count these orbits for orthogonal groups. Solving this is the first goal of this paper, in Section 4.

Our second goal is to present an algorithm for generating representatives for all rational nilpotent orbits of orthogonal and special orthogonal groups over $k$ , in the spirit of the one presented by Collingwood and McGovern in [9] over $\mathbb{R}$ ; our solution is presented in Section 5.

Our third and most important goal is to offer insight into the geometric parametrization of rational nilpotent orbits by elements of the Bruhat-Tits building of $G$ that was proposed by DeBacker in [10]. To this end we prove, in the more general setting of $G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}(D)$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{n}(D)$ (for $D$ a central division algebra over $k$ ) and classical groups, that DeBacker’s “building set” attached to a Lie triple can be identified with the building of the centralizer of that Lie triple. This kind of “functoriality result” gives a coherent interpretation of the geometry of the DeBacker parametrization, and is presented in Section 6.

Finally, combining these results, we attach a representative of each nilpotent orbit to a facet of the building in our standard apartment, and prove that this gives an explicit realization of the DeBacker correspondence, in Section 7.

Let us now summarize the results of this paper in more detail.

For symplectic, orthogonal or special orthogonal groups the algebraic nilpotent orbits can be parametrized by partitions. Let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ in which even parts occur with even multiplicity and let $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}$ denote the corresponding nilpotent adjoint orbit of the algebraic group $\mathbf{O}_{n}$ . For $i\in\mathbb{N}$ let $\chi_{i}$ be the number of odd parts of $\lambda$ whose multiplicity is exactly $i$ . Set ${\chi_{3+}}:=\sum_{i\geq 3}\chi_{i}$ .

Let $(q,V)$ be a quadratic space; then $\mathbf{O}(q)$ is a fixed $k$ -form of $\mathbf{O}_{n}$ with respect to which we take the $k$ -points of this orbit. Assume the characteristic of $k$ is either zero or sufficiently large (see Section 3) and that $p\neq 2$ . Then it is known that the rational orbits occurring $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ are parametrized by certain tuples $\mathsf{q}$ of quadratic forms (Theorem 3.2). Our first result is to compute their number.

#### Theorem (Theorem 4.3).

Let $(q,V)$ be a nondegenerate $n$ -dimensional quadratic space of anisotropic dimension ${n_{\circ}}\leq n$ . Then the number of $k$ -rational orbits under $\mathrm{O}(q)$ in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ is

$$ \mathsf{T}(q)_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},{\chi_{3+}}}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}}&\text{if ${\chi_{3+}}\geq 1$};\\
\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}&\text{if ${\chi_{3+}}=0$, ${\chi_{1}}\geq 1$};\\
\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{{\chi_{2}}}\rceil+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},{\chi_{2}}}&\text{if ${\chi_{1}}={\chi_{3+}}=0$},\end{cases} $$

where $\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},{\chi_{2}}}=0$ unless either ${n_{\circ}}=0$ and ${\chi_{2}}$ is even, or ${n_{\circ}}=4$ and ${\chi_{2}}$ is odd, in which cases $\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},{\chi_{2}}}=(-1)^{{\chi_{2}}}$ . The number of $k$ -rational orbits in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ under $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ is the same unless ${\chi_{1}}={\chi_{2}}={\chi_{3+}}={n_{\circ}}=0$ , when there are two.

The arithmetic complexity of this answer stands in sharp contrast to the cases of $\mathrm{SL}(n)$ and $\mathrm{Sp}(2n)$ . The number of $\mathrm{SL}(n,k)$ -orbits in one algebraic nilpotent orbit of $\mathrm{SL}(n)$ is $|k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{g}|$ where $g$ is the gcd of the parts of the corresponding partition. The number of $\mathrm{Sp}(2n,k)$ orbits in the algebraic orbit of $\mathrm{Sp}(2n)$ corresponding to a partition $\lambda$ is simply $4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}}$ where now $\chi_{i}$ counts the number of even parts of $\lambda$ with multiplicity exactly $i$ [19].

Next, for each pair $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})$ parametrizing a rational nilpotent orbit of $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ , we choose, following Proposition 5.1, a partition $\Gamma$ of the set $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}:=\{(i,j)\mid i\in\lambda,\,1\leq j\leq m_{i}\}$ , where $m_{i}$ denotes the multiplicity of $i$ in $\lambda$ . We construct an explicit orbit representative and associated Jacobson-Morozov triple ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ by constructing subspaces of $V$ for each part of $\Gamma$ in Sections 5.3 to 5.9. This kind of explicit parametrization has many uses in representation theory, including: computing Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms as in [1] and [14]; geometrizing invariant distributions coming from nilpotent orbits [8]; and proving the motivic nature of Shalika germs as in [13], building on work of [11]. Note that although determining a complete set of representatives in the case of special linear and symplectic groups is a direct generalization of the real case (see [19]), orthogonal and special orthogonal groups present a special challenge, and this result is not straightforward.

Using a “generalized Bala-Carter” philosophy, DeBacker parametrized the rational nilpotent orbits of groups over, among others, local non-archimedean fields (with restrictions on residual characteristic) using the Bruhat-Tits building of the corresponding group. The key construction is of a “building set” of a Lie triple $\{Y,H,X\}$ , denoted $\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)$ . Namely, the DeBacker parametrization attaches to each rational nilpotent orbit $\mathcal{O}$ one or more degenerate pairs, which for our purposes we may take to be pairs $(\mathcal{F},X)$ , where $\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)$ where $\mathcal{F}$ is a facet and $\{Y,H,X\}$ is a Lie triple extending a representative $X$ of $\mathcal{O}$ (see Section 7). When $\mathcal{F}$ is maximal in $\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)$ , the pair is called distinguished; associativity classes of distinguished pairs are in bijection with rational nilpotent orbits [10]. The challenge inherent in this description is that it does not suffice to work within a single apartment: a facet $\mathcal{F}$ of the building may be maximal in $\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)\cap\mathcal{A}$ without being distinguished!

We prove the following general result in Section 6. Here $D$ denotes a central division algebra over $k$ , $\mathcal{R}$ denotes the integer ring of $k$ , and $p$ is sufficiently large (see Section 3).

#### Theorem (Theorem 6.1).

Suppose $G$ is $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(D)$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{n}(D)$ or a classical group, and suppose ${\mathrm{d}\phi}=\{Y,H,X\}$ is a Lie triple in $\mathfrak{g}$ , with corresponding homomorphism $\phi\colon\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k)\to G$ . Let $G^{\phi}$ be the centralizer of $\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k))$ in $G$ . Then $\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)=\mathcal{B}(G)^{\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R}))}$ and there is a $G^{\phi}$ -equivariant identification

$$ \mathcal{B}(G)^{\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R}))}=\mathcal{B}(G^{\phi}). $$

An immediate consequence is a formula for the dimension of all the maximal facets in $\mathcal{B}(Y,H,X)$ , whence it suffices to produce a pair $(\mathcal{F},X)$ attached to $\mathcal{O}$ of the correct dimension in order to deduce that it is distinguished. We apply this approach to prove the correctness of our parametrization for orthogonal and special orthogonal groups in Proposition 7.1 and Theorem 7.2.

DeBacker’s parametrization has only been explored in a handful of cases, including [19] for the special linear and symplectic groups, where the dimensions of the maximal facets were established via combinatorial arguments.

The current paper initially arose from an NSERC USRA project of T. Bernstein, working under the supervision of M. Nevins, on counting the number of rational nilpotent orbits for orthogonal groups. M. Nevins complemented this with a parametrization of these orbits and circulated a preprint, whereupon the J.-J. Ma and J.W. Yap shared their report [22]. In it, J.W. Yap, working under the supervision of J.-J. Ma, constructs distinguished representatives of rational nilpotent orbits of split even orthogonal groups (correcting also an error in the proof of [19, Theorem 4]), and proves Theorem 6.1 in that case. They had also gone on to prove Theorem 6.1 as it appears here. J.-J. Ma would like to thank J.K. Yu for many helpful discussions on this topic.

Several interesting questions remain open.

For one, although the proof of Theorem 6.1 is currently restricted to particular groups, J.-J. Ma has shown separately the existence of the map $\mathscr{R}\colon\mathcal{B}(G)^{\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R}))}\to\mathcal{B}(G^{\phi})$ (6.1) for any connected semisimple $\mathbf{G}$ of adjoint type over $k$ , and conjectures that there should be a natural inverse map $\mathscr{E}$ .

For another, it is an open question to determine known invariants of rational nilpotent orbits in terms of the data of their DeBacker parametrization. Together with [19], we now have the complete parametrization for all split classical groups, which opens the possibilities for study. Part of the problem would be to give a combinatorial description of the associativity classes of facets in $\mathcal{B}$ , and more particularly of the $r$ -associativity classes for each $r\in\mathbb{R}$ , which are greater in number and offer a finer parametrization.

Our counting results rely on Jacobson-Morozov theory to describe the nilpotent orbits, and thus entail a restriction on the characteristic of $k$ . It would be interesting to count rational orbits, and give explicit representatives, in these missing cases.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we establish our notation and some necessary results about quadratic forms. In Section 3 we give the constraints on the characteristic and residual characteristic for the union of the results in this paper, and review key facts about nilpotent orbits and the orthogonal groups. Section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 4.3, counting the number of rational orbits. In Section 5, we present an algorithm for generating representatives of each orbit. To do so explicitly, we set the notation for root vectors in Section 5.1 and describe the overall strategy in Section 5.2, with details for each of the subcases in Sections 5.3 to 5.9. In Section 6 we revert to the case of general $G$ and briefly recall the DeBacker parametrization, before proving Theorem 6.1. In Section 7 we attach to each of our orbit representatives a distinguished pair, thus establishing a new dictionary from the partition-based to the building-based parametrizations of rational nilpotent orbits for orthogonal and special orthogonal groups.

## 2. Notation and the Witt group

Let $k$ be a local non-archimedean field of residual characteristic $p\neq 2$ , with integer ring $\mathcal{R}$ and maximal ideal $\mathcal{P}$ generated by a uniformizer $\varpi$ . Denote by $\mathfrak{f}$ the residue field of $k$ . Let $\rho$ be a fixed nonsquare in $\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ with image $\rho_{\mathfrak{f}}$ in $\mathfrak{f}^{\times}$ .

The following theory is concisely presented in [2] and based on [15, Chapter 1]. A quadratic space $(q,V)$ over a field $F$ such that $\textrm{char}(F)\neq 2$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over $F$ equipped with a regular quadratic form $q$ ; when needed, its associated (nondegenerate) bilinear form is denoted $B_{q}$ , a matrix form is $M_{q}$ , and the dimension of $V$ is $\deg(q)$ , the degree of $q$ . Denote by $\mathcal{H}$ the quadratic hyperbolic plane.

If $(q,V)$ and $(q^{\prime},V^{\prime})$ are two quadratic spaces we write $q\cong q^{\prime}$ if they are isometric and $q\simeq q^{\prime}$ if the isometry classes of the quadratic forms $q$ and $q^{\prime}$ differ by a sum of hyperbolic planes. Then $\simeq$ defines an equivalence relation on the monoid of nondegenerate quadratic forms, and the resulting quotient is the Witt group $\mathcal{W}_{F}$ of $F$ with trivial element denoted $\overline{0}$ or $\mathcal{H}$ . Write $\overline{q}$ for the image of $q$ in $\mathcal{W}_{F}$ , which we can identify up to isometry with the anisotropic kernel $q_{\circ}$ of $q$ . Then $\dim\overline{q}:=\deg(q_{\circ})={n_{\circ}}$ is the anisotropic dimension of $q$ .

Each quadratic space $(q,V)$ admits a basis relative to which $q$ is diagonalized; in this case we write $q=\langle a_{1},\cdots,a_{n}\rangle$ for some $a_{i}\in F^{\times}$ but even up to permuting and scaling each coordinate by elements of $(F^{\times})^{2}$ this representation of $q$ is not necessarily unique.

If $F=\mathfrak{f}$ , then since $p>2$ we have $\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}=\{\mathcal{H},\langle 1\rangle,\langle\rho_{\mathfrak{f}}\rangle,\langle 1,-\rho_{\mathfrak{f}}\rangle\}$ , which has the structure of $\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{-}\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{2}$ if $-1\in k^{2}$ (that is, if $p$ is congruent to $1$ mod $4$ ) and of $\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+}\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ otherwise. The identification of sets $\iota\colon\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{-}\to\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+}$ is thus not a homomorphism but it is easy to check that it satisfies the very useful property that for all $\mathsf{u},{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{-}$ ,

$$ \dim(\iota(\mathsf{u})-\iota({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}))=\dim(\iota(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})). $$

If $F=k$ , then the map $\rho_{\mathfrak{f}}\mapsto\rho$ induces a well-defined injection $i\colon\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}\to\mathcal{W}_{k}$ . In fact, the map which sends $(\mathsf{u},{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{2}$ to the class of $i(\mathsf{u})\oplus\varpi i({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ defines an isomorphism $\mathcal{W}_{k}\cong\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{2}$ . (We may write $\mathcal{W}_{k}^{\pm}$ when we want to specify the group structure.)

#### Lemma 2.1.

Let $k$ be a local non-archimedean field of odd residual characteristic.

- 1. The number of isometry classes of quadratic forms of degree $n$ is $4$ if $n=1$ , $7$ if $n=2$ , and $8$ if $n\geq 3$ .

- 2. The number of choices of distinct diagonal representations of each anisotropic form or hyperbolic plane, counting order but modulo $(k^{\times})^{2}$ , is an invariant of the anisotropic dimension and is independent of the class of $p$ mod $4$ .

- 3. The map $\iota$ extends to a bijection $\iota\colon\mathcal{W}_{k}^{-}\to\mathcal{W}_{k}^{+}$ such that for all $\mathsf{u},{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}^{-}$ , (2.2)

$$ \dim(\iota(\mathsf{u})-\iota({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}))=\dim(\iota(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})). $$

#### Proof.

The first statement is well-known, but can also be inferred from Table 1 directly. We have recorded the number of choices of distinct diagonal representatives for each class of anisotropic form or hyperbolic plane, counting order but modulo scaling in each factor by $(k^{\times})^{2}$ , in the fourth column of Table 1; this establishes the second assertion. The map $\iota$ extends via the isomorphisms $i\colon\mathcal{W}_{k}^{\pm}\to(\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{\pm})^{2}$ . Since $\dim(i(\mathsf{u})\oplus\varpi i({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}))=\dim(\mathsf{u})\oplus\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ for any $\mathsf{u},{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathfrak{f}}$ , (2.2) follows from (2.1). For convenience, we have recorded the common representatives defining the map $\iota$ in the last column of Table 1. ∎

We say that two tuples of quadratic forms $(q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{s})$ and $(q_{1}^{\prime},q_{2}^{\prime},\ldots,q_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime})$ are isometric if $s=s^{\prime}$ and for all $i$ , $q_{i}\cong q_{i}^{\prime}$ . Let $\mathsf{q}=[q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{s}]$ denote the corresponding isometry class; then $\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q_{1}}+\cdots+\overline{q_{s}}$ is a well-defined element of $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ . We say that $\mathsf{q}$ represents $q$ if $\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q}$ .

Now let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ . The multiplicity $m_{i}$ of $i$ in $\lambda$ is number of times $i$ occurs in $\lambda$ . Let $\Lambda^{e}(n)$ denote the set of partitions of $n$ in which even parts occur with even multiplicity. For $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ , let $\mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}=\{\mathcal{H}\}$ if $\lambda$ has no odd parts; otherwise, let $j_{1}<j_{2}<\ldots<j_{s}$ denote its distinct odd parts and let

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}=\{\mathsf{q}:=[q_{1},\ldots,q_{s}]\mid\text{for each $i$, $q_{i}$ is a quadratic form of degree $m_{j_{i}}$}\} $$

be the set of isometry classes of $s$ -tuples of quadratic forms of the stated degrees.

Given a quadratic space $(q,V)$ of degree $n$ , we set

$$ \mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)=\{(\lambda,\mathsf{q})\mid\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n),\mathsf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}\text{\; such that \;}\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q}\}. $$

If $n$ is even, let $\Lambda^{ve}(n)\subset\Lambda^{e}(n)$ be the subset of partitions of $n$ which have no odd parts; these are called very even partitions. If $\overline{q}=\overline{0}$ then to each very even partition we attach two distinct copies of $\mathcal{H}$ , to give

$$ \mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)=\mathcal{N}(\overline{0},n)\sqcup\{(\lambda,\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\mid\lambda\in\Lambda^{ve}(n)\}. $$

## 3. Lie triples, nilpotent adjoint orbits, and the orthogonal group

Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a semisimple algebraic group defined over $k$ and $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ its Lie algebra. Let $h$ be the maximal value of the Coxeter number of any irreducible component of the root system of $\mathbf{G}$ . We assume that the characteristic of $k$ is either zero, or else is greater than $3(h-1)$ . This hypothesis implies, by [7, §5.5], that each Lie triple defined below lifts to a unique homomorphism of algebraic groups $\phi\colon{\mathbf{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}}\to\mathbf{G}$ , and that the degree of nilpotency of any nilpotent element is less than $p$ . Hence, if $\mathrm{char}(k)=p$ , then for each nilpotent element $X\in\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ , we have $X^{[p]}=0$ where this denotes the $p$ -operation on the restricted Lie algebra $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ . We note that by the work of G. McNinch, including particularly [16], these hypotheses on $p$ can often be weakened via the theory of optimal $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -homomorphisms.

### 3.1. Lie triples

Let $G=\mathbf{G}(k)$ and $\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})(k)$ . A Lie triple is a nonzero set $\{Y,H,X\}\subset\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ such that $[H,X]=2X$ , $[H,Y]=-2Y$ and $[X,Y]=H$ . Then Jacobson-Morozov theory [3, VIII,§11], [16] asserts a bijection between the nonzero nilpotent orbits of $\mathbf{G}$ on $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ (respectively, of $G$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ ) and conjugacy classes of Lie triples in $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})$ under $\mathbf{G}$ (respectively, in $\mathfrak{g}$ under $G$ ), given by associating the triple to the orbit of its nilpositive element $X$ . Moreover, by [7, §5.5] there is a group homomorphism $\phi\colon{\mathbf{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}}\to\mathbf{G}$ defined over $k$ for which

$$ {\mathrm{d}\phi}\left(\left[\begin{matrix}0&0\\
1&0\end{matrix}\right]\right)=Y,\ {\mathrm{d}\phi}\left(\left[\begin{matrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{matrix}\right]\right)=H,\;\text{and}\;{\mathrm{d}\phi}\left(\left[\begin{matrix}0&1\\
0&0\end{matrix}\right]\right)=X. $$

We often denote the Lie triple $\{Y,H,X\}$ by ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ .

Suppose $V$ is a $G$ -module; then the subgroup $\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k))$ (or equivalently its Lie algebra ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ ) decomposes $V$ into pairwise orthogonal isotypic components. Let $U_{i}$ denote the unique irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -module of degree $i$ , and set $M^{i}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)}(U_{i},V)$ . Then for each $i$ the map sending $(u,T)\in U_{i}\otimes M^{i}$ to $T(u)\in V$ induces an isomorphism

$$ V=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}V_{i}\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}U_{i}\otimes M^{i}, $$

where $V_{i}$ is the $U_{i}$ -isotypic component of $V$ . Since elements of $G^{\phi}$ commute with ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ , each space $M^{i}$ is a $G^{\phi}$ -module.

In Section 6, we have need of the preceding in the more general setting of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R})$ -modules. For each $n<p$ let $\mathcal{U}_{n}$ be the irreducible module of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R})$ of rank $n+1$ . Then $U_{n}=\mathcal{U}_{n}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}k$ and $\mathbb{U}_{n}:=\mathcal{U}_{n}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathfrak{f}:=\mathcal{U}_{n}/\mathcal{P}\mathcal{U}_{n}$ . For any $\mathcal{R}$ -lattice $\mathcal{L}$ , let $L:=\mathcal{L}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}k$ and $\mathbb{L}:=\mathcal{L}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathfrak{f}$ .

#### Lemma 3.1.

Suppose $\mathcal{L}$ is an $\mathcal{R}$ -lattice with $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R})$ -action given by $\phi$ . Then

$$ \mathcal{L}\cong\bigoplus_{i<p}\mathcal{U}_{i}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}{\mathcal{M}^{i}} $$

where ${\mathcal{M}^{i}}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R})}(\mathcal{U}_{i},\mathcal{L})$ is an $\mathcal{R}$ -lattice in $M^{i}$ .

#### Proof.

By the assumption on $p$ , the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathfrak{f})$ -module $\mathbb{L}$ is semisimple, and therefore $\mathbb{L}\cong\bigoplus_{i<p}\mathbb{U}_{i}\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathfrak{f})}(\mathbb{U}_{i},\mathbb{L})$ . It now follows from [17, Proposition 5.3.1] that this isomorphism lifts to the level of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{R})$ -modules. ∎

### 3.2. Centralizers

Under the hypotheses on $k$ , the centralizer $G^{\phi}$ of $\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k))$ in $G$ coincides with $G^{{\mathrm{d}\phi}}$ , the stabilizer under the adjoint action of the Lie triple ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ . Let us describe the structure of $G^{\phi}$ for a large class of groups.

Let $D$ be a central division algebra over $k$ and suppose $V$ is additionally a right $D$ -module. Then $M^{i}$ inherits the structure of a right $D$ -module. In fact, if $G=\mathrm{GL}(V,D)$ then $G^{\phi}\cong\prod_{i}\mathrm{GL}(M^{i},D)$ .

Now suppose further that $V$ is equipped with a non-degenerate $G$ -invariant sesquilinear form $F$ . Let $\beta_{i}$ denote the the unique (up to scaling) $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -invariant nondegenerate bilinear form on $U_{i}$ . It is symplectic if $i$ is even and symmetric if $i$ is odd. In this latter case, fix a choice of form such that $\beta_{i}(\mathcal{U}_{i},\mathcal{U}_{i})=\mathcal{R}$ and $q_{\beta_{i}}\cong\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus k}$ where $i=2k+1$ .

Then under the isomorphism (3.2), for each $i$ , $F$ and $\beta_{i}$ induce a nondegenerate $G^{\phi}$ -invariant form $\gamma^{i}$ on $M^{i}$ which satisfies, for each $u,u^{\prime}\in U_{i}$ and each $T,T^{\prime}\in M^{i}$ , that $F(T(u),T^{\prime}(u^{\prime}))=\beta_{i}(u,u^{\prime})\gamma^{i}(T,T^{\prime})$ . It follows that if $G$ is the group $\mathrm{U}(V,F)$ of isometries of $(V,F)$ , then $G^{\phi}\cong\prod_{i}\mathrm{U}(M^{i},\gamma^{i})$ .

In the special case that $D=k$ and $F$ is a symmetric bilinear form, we have that $\gamma^{i}$ is symplectic for each even $i$ and symmetric for each odd $i$ . Writing $O(q):=\mathrm{U}(V,B_{q})$ for any quadratic space $(V,q)$ and $\mathrm{Sp}(n):=\mathrm{U}(V,F)$ for any symplectic space $(V,F)$ of dimension $n$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{O}(q)^{\phi}\cong\prod_{\text{$i$ odd: $M^{i}\neq 0$}}\mathrm{O}(q_{\gamma^{i}})\times\prod_{\text{$i$ even: $M^{i}\neq 0$}}\mathrm{Sp}(\dim(M^{i})). $$

### 3.3. Nilpotent orbits of orthogonal groups and algebras

For the remainder of this section and until Section 6, let $D=k$ and $F=B_{q}$ be symmetric, so that $(q,V)$ is an $n$ -dimensional quadratic space over $k$ . The special orthogonal Lie algebra is

$$ \mathfrak{so}(q)=\{X\in\mathfrak{sl}(n,k)\mid{}^{t}XM_{q}+M_{q}X=0\}. $$

Observe that $\mathfrak{so}(q)=\mathfrak{so}(\alpha q)$ for any $\alpha\in k^{\times}$ , so from Table 1 we infer there is a single isomorphism class of Lie algebra for each anisotropic dimension, except for $\dim\overline{q}=2$ . In this latter case, by the Kneser-Tits classification [20], there are two isomorphism classes, corresponding to Lie algebras splitting over a ramified or an unramified extension respectively. The orthogonal group is

$$ \mathrm{O}(q)=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}(n,k)\mid{}^{t}gM_{q}g=M_{q}\} $$

and it contains $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ as the index-two subgroup of elements of determinant equal to $1$ . These groups are compact if and only if $q$ is anisotropic. We think of them as the $k$ -points of the corresponding inner forms of the algebraic groups $\mathbf{O}_{n}$ and $\mathbf{SO}_{n}$ , respectively.

Given a geometric nilpotent orbit $\mathcal{O}$ under the algebraic group $\mathbf{O}(q)\cong\mathbf{O}_{n}$ , then its set of rational points $\mathcal{O}(k)$ may be empty, or may decompose as a union of one or more rational nilpotent orbits. In the latter case, using the arguments of [18, Prop 4.1], one can deduce that the set of rational orbits is in bijection with the kernel of the map of pointed sets in Galois cohomology

$$ \alpha\colon H^{1}(k,\mathbf{O}(q)^{\phi})\to H^{1}(k,\mathbf{O}(q)) $$

where ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ is an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple for a base point of $\mathcal{O}$ and $\mathbf{O}(q)^{\phi}$ is its centralizer.

By (3.3), the algebraic group $\mathbf{O}(q)^{\phi}$ is a product of symplectic and orthogonal groups. For a group $U$ preserving a nondegenerate $m$ -dimensional bilinear form, $H^{1}(k,U)$ counts the number of $k$ -isometry classes of forms of degree $m$ ; thus it is trivial if the form is symplectic, and if the form is symmetric, it has order $4$ , $7$ or $8$ if $m$ is $1$ , $2$ or at least $3$ , respectively. The kernel of the map (3.4) can thus parametrized by tuples of quadratic forms whose sum is equivalent to the chosen form $q$ in the Witt group. This correspondence is made explicit in the proof of the following theorem, which is a known result; for example, for $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ see [9, Ch. 9] and for extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ see [21, I.6].

#### Theorem 3.2.

Let $(q,V)$ be a nondegenerate $n$ -dimensional quadratic space over $k$ . The nilpotent $\mathrm{O}(q)$ orbits on $\mathfrak{so}(q)$ are parametrized by the set $\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ . If $\overline{q}\neq\overline{0}$ , then the nilpotent $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ orbits coincide with those under $\mathrm{O}(q)$ but otherwise, $n$ is even and the nilpotent $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ -orbits are parametrized by the set $\mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $X\in\mathfrak{so}(q)\setminus\{0\}$ be nilpotent and let ${\mathrm{d}\phi}=\{Y,H,X\}$ be a corresponding Lie triple. Decompose $V$ into isotypic components under the corresponding action of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ (or equivalently under its lift $\phi(\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k))$ ) as in (3.2); then the nonzero summands are indexed by parts $i$ of a partition $\lambda$ of $n$ in which each part $i$ occurs with multiplicity $m_{i}=\dim(M^{i})$ . Hence $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ , since even parts correspond to symplectic forms. If $X=\{0\}$ set ${\mathrm{d}\phi}=\{0\}$ and $M^{1}=V$ in (3.2), so that $\lambda=[1^{n}]$ . When $i$ is an odd part of $\lambda$ , we have $q_{\beta_{i}}\simeq\langle 1\rangle$ . Thus writing $q_{i}:=q|_{V_{i}}$ and noting that $q_{\beta_{i}}\otimes q_{\gamma^{i}}\cong q_{i}$ , we conclude that $(q_{\gamma^{i}},M^{i})\simeq(q_{i},V_{i})$ in $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ . On the other hand, when $i$ is an even part of $\lambda$ , $\beta_{i}\otimes\gamma^{i}$ is a split quadratic space, whence $(q_{i},V_{i})\simeq\mathcal{H}$ in $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ .

Consequently, the tuple $\mathsf{q}=[q_{\gamma^{j}}\mid\text{$j$ odd, $m_{j}\neq 0$}]$ lies in $\mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}$ . Since $\oplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}q_{i}\simeq q$ , the pair $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})$ lies in $\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ . Since $G^{\phi}$ acts by isometries on the spaces $M^{i}$ , this map ${\mathrm{d}\phi}\to\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ lifts to a well-defined map on nilpotent orbits. It is surjective, since each element of $\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ defines a decomposition (3.2) of $(q,V)$ (uniquely up to isometry) and consequently a subgroup of $\mathrm{O}(q)$ isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k)$ .

To show this map is bijective, suppose ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ and ${\mathrm{d}\phi}^{\prime}$ are two Lie triples in $\mathfrak{so}(q)$ and $V=\oplus_{i}V_{i}$ and $V=\oplus_{i}V_{i}^{\prime}$ are the corresponding decompositions of $V$ into isotypic components. Then these decompositions are isometric if and only if ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ and ${\mathrm{d}\phi}^{\prime}$ are conjugate via an element of $\mathrm{O}(q)$ . As $\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ is in bijection with the set of isometry classes of such decompositions, the first statement of the theorem follows.

To understand the $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ orbits, suppose that $g\in\mathrm{O}(q)\setminus\mathrm{SO}(q)$ gives $\mathrm{Ad}(g){\mathrm{d}\phi}={\mathrm{d}\phi}^{\prime}$ . From (3.3), and that the symplectic factors have determinant $1$ , we conclude that $\mathrm{O}(q)^{\phi}$ contains an element $h$ of determinant $-1$ if and only if $\lambda$ contains at least one odd part, in which case $gh\in\mathrm{SO}(q)$ and $\mathrm{Ad}(gh){\mathrm{d}\phi}={\mathrm{d}\phi}^{\prime}$ , showing that the $\mathrm{O}(q)$ and $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ orbits coincide.

If, however, $\dim(V_{i})$ is even for all $i$ , then no such $h$ exists. In this case, each $V_{i}$ is a split quadratic space and so $(q,V)$ is a sum of hyperbolic planes, whence $\overline{q}=0$ . Since $\mathrm{O}(q)^{\phi}=\mathrm{SO}(q)^{\phi}$ in this case, and $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ has index two in $\mathrm{O}(q)$ , we deduce that each of the $\mathrm{O}(q)$ -orbits corresponding to $\lambda\in\Lambda^{ve}(n)$ decompose as a disjoint union of two $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ -orbits. ∎

Note that for $i$ odd, where convenient, we can and do identify $M^{i}$ with the $0$ -weight space of $V_{i}$ .

## 4. Counting rational nilpotent orbits

Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ . For $i\in\mathbb{N}$ let $\chi_{i}$ denote the number of odd parts $j$ of $\lambda$ occurring with multiplicity exactly $i$ , and set ${\chi_{3+}}=\sum_{i=3}^{n}\chi_{i}$ . Let $X$ be an element of the algebraic orbit $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}$ , ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ an associated Lie triple, and $\phi$ the corresponding homomorphism $\phi\colon\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathbf{O}(q)$ . From the form of $\mathbf{O}(q)^{\phi}$ in (3.3), and Lemma 2.1, we deduce that

$$ |H^{1}(k,\mathbf{O}(q)^{\phi})|=4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}}, $$

whereas $|H^{1}(k,\mathbf{O}(q))|\in\{4,7,8\}$ , depending on $n$ . Thus from the discussion preceding the statement of Theorem 3.2, if $n\geq 3$ one expects for each choice of $k$ -form $\mathbf{O}(q)$ about $\frac{1}{8}(4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}})$ rational orbits in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ , with some variation depending on $\lambda$ and $q$ .

On the other hand, Theorem 3.2 gives a direct means of counting the number of rational orbits in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ : they are parametrized by $P_{\lambda,q}=\{\mathsf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}\mid\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q}\}$ . That is to say, it suffices to count the number of isometry classes of tuples (of degrees prescribed by the multiplicities of the odd parts in $\lambda$ ) that represent $\overline{q}$ . This is a nontrivial counting problem, and the subject of this section.

We begin with the simple case that each odd part of $\lambda$ has multiplicity equal to $1$ .

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $\mathsf{u}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ and let ${n_{\circ}}$ be its anisotropic dimension ${n_{\circ}}=\dim(\mathsf{u})$ . Let ${\chi_{1}}\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ have the same parity as ${n_{\circ}}$ . The number $\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}}}$ of isometry classes of ${\chi_{1}}$ -tuples of degree-one quadratic forms representing $\mathsf{u}$ is

$$ \mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}}}=\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}. $$

#### Proof.

For ease of notation set $\chi:={\chi_{1}}$ . We prove this formula by induction on even and odd $\chi$ , respectively. When $\chi=1$ , we have $N(\mathsf{u})_{1}=1$ if ${n_{\circ}}=1$ but $N(\mathsf{u})_{1}=0$ if ${n_{\circ}}=3$ , so (4.1) holds. When $\chi=2$ , there are $16$ distinct isometry classes of pairs of quadratic forms. By Lemma 2.1, regardless of the sign of $-1$ in $k$ , each of the six anisotropic quadratic forms $\mathsf{u}$ with ${n_{\circ}}=2$ is represented by exactly two such pairs, accounting for $12=6\times 2$ pairs; the remaining four pairs represent the hyperbolic plane (which has ${n_{\circ}}=0$ ). In particular no pair can represent $\mathcal{Q}_{4}$ (which has ${n_{\circ}}=4$ ). This count agrees with (4.1) for $\chi=2$ and each ${n_{\circ}}\in\{0,2,4\}$ . Thus (4.1) holds for $\chi\in\{1,2\}$ and all $\mathsf{u}$ with ${n_{\circ}}$ of the same parity as $\chi$ .

Suppose now that $\chi>2$ and that $\mathsf{N}({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{\chi-2}$ satisfies (4.1) for all ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ such that ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}:=\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ has the same parity as $\chi$ . In particular, since the right side of (4.1) depends only on the anisotropic dimension, we may define $\mathsf{N}({n^{\prime}_{\circ}})_{\chi-2}:=\mathsf{N}({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{\chi-2}$ .

Let $\mathsf{u}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ and suppose it is represented by a $\chi$ -tuple of degree-one quadratic forms $\mathsf{q}_{\chi}=[q_{1},q_{2},\mathsf{q}_{\chi-2}]$ where $\mathsf{q}_{\chi-2}$ denotes an $(\chi-2)$ -tuple. Set ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\overline{\mathsf{q}_{\chi-2}}$ ; then ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathsf{u}-\overline{\langle q_{1},q_{2}\rangle}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ . Set ${n_{\circ}}=\dim(\mathsf{u})$ and ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ ; then necessarily ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}\in\{{n_{\circ}},{n_{\circ}}\pm 2\}\cap\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ .

Suppose first that ${n_{\circ}}\in\{0,4\}$ . There are four pairs that yield $\langle q_{1},q_{2}\rangle\simeq\mathcal{H}$ (and hence give ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathsf{u}$ and thus ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}={n_{\circ}}$ ) whereas the twelve others give ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=2$ , yielding

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi} \displaystyle=4\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi-2}+12\mathsf{N}(2)_{\chi-2} \displaystyle=4(\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi-2}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{\chi-4})+12(\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi-2})=\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{\chi-2}. $$

Next suppose that ${n_{\circ}}=2$ . Then for each ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\{\mathcal{H},\mathcal{Q}_{4}\}$ we have that $\dim(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})=2$ , so $\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ is represented by exactly two choices of pairs $(q_{1},q_{2})$ . Thus the remaining $12$ choices of $(q_{1},q_{2})$ correspond to ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ such that ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=2$ . This yields

$$ \mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi}=2\mathsf{N}(0)_{\chi-2}+12\mathsf{N}(2)_{\chi-2}+2\mathsf{N}(4)_{\chi-2}=16(\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi-2})=\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi}, $$

as required.

Finally, suppose ${n_{\circ}}\in\{1,3\}$ . If ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathsf{u}$ , then we must have $\langle q_{1},q_{2}\rangle\simeq\mathcal{H}$ ; this accounts for $4$ pairs $(q_{1},q_{2})$ . For each of the three other elements ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ of the same anisotropic dimension as $\mathsf{u}$ , a quick calculation using Table 1 and Lemma 2.1 yields that $\dim(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})=2$ and so $\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ is representable by exactly two choices of $(q_{1},q_{2})$ . This accounts for $3\times 2=6$ pairs. The remaining six choices of $(q_{1},q_{2})$ therefore yield ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ such that ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}\neq{n_{\circ}}$ , so necessarily ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=4-{n_{\circ}}$ . We thus infer

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi} \displaystyle=4\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi-2}+6\mathsf{N}({n_{\circ}})_{\chi-2}+6\mathsf{N}(4-{n_{\circ}})_{\chi-2} \displaystyle=10(\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi-2}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{\chi-4})+6(\frac{1}{8}4^{\chi-2}+({n_{\circ}}-2)2^{\chi-4}), $$

and the formula follows. ∎

Now consider the case that each odd part of $\lambda$ has multiplicity exactly two.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $\mathsf{u}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ be such that $\dim(\mathsf{u})={n_{\circ}}\in\{0,2,4\}$ , and let ${\chi_{2}}\geq 0$ . Then the number $\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{2}}}$ of isometry classes of ${\chi_{2}}$ -tuples of degree-two quadratic forms representing $\mathsf{u}$ is

$$ \mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{2}}}=\begin{cases}\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{\chi_{2}}\rceil+1&\text{if ${\chi_{2}}$ is even and ${n_{\circ}}=0$};\\
\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{\chi_{2}}\rceil-1&\text{if ${\chi_{2}}$ is odd and ${n_{\circ}}=4$};\\
\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{\chi_{2}}\rceil&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

where $\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{\chi_{2}}\rceil=\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi_{2}}-(-1)^{\chi_{2}})$ denotes the closest integer to $7^{\chi_{2}}/8$ .

#### Proof.

Set $\chi:={\chi_{2}}$ . We can write the formula as $\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi}=\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi}-(-1)^{\chi})+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi},$ where

$$ \varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{\chi}&\text{if ${n_{\circ}}=0$ and $\chi$ is even, or ${n_{\circ}}=4$ and $\chi$ is odd, and}\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Notice that if ${n_{\circ}}\in\{0,4\}$ then $\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi-1}+(-1)^{\chi}=\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi}$ , for all $\chi$ .

When $\chi=0$ , then $\mathsf{M}(\overline{0})_{0}=1$ and $\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{0}=0$ for all $\mathsf{u}\neq\overline{0}$ so the formula holds. Assume $\chi\geq 1$ and let us count the number of ways, up to isometry, to construct a $\chi$ -tuple of degree-two quadratic forms $\mathsf{q}_{\chi}=[q_{1},\mathsf{q}_{\chi-1}]$ representing $\mathsf{u}$ . There are $7$ choices for the form $q_{1}$ , of which $6$ are anisotropic. Set ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\overline{\mathsf{q}_{\chi-1}}=\mathsf{u}-\overline{q_{1}}$ and let ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ . By induction $\mathsf{M}({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{\chi-1}$ is an invariant of anisotropic dimension so we can set $\mathsf{M}({n^{\prime}_{\circ}})_{\chi-1}:=\mathsf{M}({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{\chi-1}$ .

Suppose ${n_{\circ}}\in\{0,4\}$ . If $\overline{q_{1}}=\overline{0}$ then ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathsf{u}$ and ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}={n_{\circ}}$ ; otherwise, ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})=\dim(\mathsf{u}-\overline{q_{1}})=2$ . Therefore we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi} \displaystyle=\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi-1}+6\mathsf{M}(2)_{\chi-1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi-1}-(-1)^{\chi-1})+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi-1}+6(\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi-1}-(-1)^{\chi-1})) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi}-(-1)^{\chi})+(-1)^{\chi}+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi-1}=\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi}-(-1)^{\chi})+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},\chi}. $$

On the other hand, if ${n_{\circ}}=2$ , then ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathcal{H}$ if $\overline{q_{1}}=\mathsf{u}$ and ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathcal{Q}_{4}$ if $\overline{q_{1}}=\mathcal{Q}_{4}-\mathsf{u}$ . Each of the remaining five choices of $\overline{q_{1}}$ gives ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ such that ${n^{\prime}_{\circ}}=2$ . This yields the final relation

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{M}(\mathsf{u})_{\chi} \displaystyle=\mathsf{M}(\mathcal{H})_{\chi-1}+5\mathsf{M}(2)_{\chi-1}+\mathsf{M}(\mathcal{Q}_{4})_{\chi-1} \displaystyle=7(\frac{1}{8}(7^{\chi-1}-(-1)^{\chi-1}))+\varepsilon_{0,\chi-1}+\varepsilon_{4,\chi-1}. $$

Since $\varepsilon_{0,\chi-1}+\varepsilon_{4,\chi-1}=(-1)^{\chi-1}$ , the formula follows. ∎

#### Theorem 4.3.

Let $M$ be a vector space of dimension $n\geq 1$ and let $A$ be an index set. Suppose $M$ is decomposed as a direct sum of nonzero subspaces $\oplus_{\alpha\in A}M_{\alpha}$ ; set $\chi_{i}=|\{\alpha\mid\dim(M_{\alpha})=i\}|$ . Let $\mathsf{u}\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ and let ${n_{\circ}}=\dim(\mathsf{u})$ denote its anisotropic dimension. If $n-{n_{\circ}}$ is a nonnegative even integer, then the number of ways $\mathsf{T}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},{\chi_{3+}}}$ of assigning a nondegenerate quadratic form to each of the $|A|$ subspaces such that the sum is equivalent to $\mathsf{u}$ in the Witt group is

$$ \mathsf{T}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},{\chi_{3+}}}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}}&\text{if ${\chi_{3+}}\geq 1$};\\
\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}&\text{if ${\chi_{3+}}=0$, ${\chi_{1}}\geq 1$};\\
\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{{\chi_{2}}}\rceil+\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},{\chi_{2}}}&\text{if ${\chi_{1}}={\chi_{3+}}=0$},\end{cases} $$

where $\varepsilon_{{n_{\circ}},{\chi_{2}}}$ was defined in (4.2).

#### Proof.

Set ${\chi_{3+}}=\sum_{i=3}^{n}\chi_{i}$ . First suppose that there exists some $\alpha\in A$ such that $\dim(M_{\alpha})\geq 3$ . Then the number of choices of quadratic forms on $M^{\prime}=\oplus_{\beta\neq\alpha}M_{\beta}$ is $4^{{\chi_{1}}}7^{{\chi_{2}}}8^{{\chi_{3+}}-1}$ . Given such a choice, let ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ be its Witt class. Then $\dim(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})$ has the same parity as $\dim(M_{\alpha})$ . Since $\dim(M_{\alpha})\geq 3$ , each of the 8 possible choices of $\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ can be realized on $M_{\alpha}$ . The formula follows.

Now suppose that ${\chi_{3+}}=0$ , so that $\dim(M_{\alpha})\in\{1,2\}$ for all $\alpha\in A$ . If ${\chi_{2}}=0$ or ${\chi_{1}}=0$ then we apply Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, respectively. Otherwise, letting $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ denote the subgroup of the Witt group of all quadratic forms of even anisotropic dimension, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{T}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},0} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{2}}\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{{\chi_{1}}}\mathsf{M}({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{{\chi_{2}}}=\sum_{{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{2}}\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{{\chi_{1}}}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{{\chi_{2}}}\right\rceil+\varepsilon_{\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}),{\chi_{2}}}\right) \displaystyle=4^{{\chi_{1}}}\left\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{{\chi_{2}}}\right\rceil+\sum_{{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W}_{2}}\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})_{{\chi_{1}}}\varepsilon_{\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}),{\chi_{2}}} $$

where at this last step we have used that $\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}$ ranges over all Witt classes of quadratic forms of dimension of the same parity as $\dim(\mathsf{u})$ , and thus all $4^{{\chi_{1}}}$ possible ${\chi_{1}}$ -tuples of degree-one quadratic forms.

When ${\chi_{2}}$ is even, $\varepsilon_{\dim({\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}),{\chi_{2}}}$ is nonzero only when ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\overline{0}$ , in which case $\varepsilon_{0,{\chi_{2}}}=1$ , so the final summand is

$$ \varepsilon_{0,{\chi_{2}}}\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}}}=\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2} $$

whereas when ${\chi_{2}}$ is odd, the only nonzero factor is $\varepsilon_{4,{\chi_{2}}}=-1$ and the term corresponding to ${\mathsf{u}^{\prime}}=\mathcal{Q}_{4}$ has $\dim(\mathsf{u}-{\mathsf{u}^{\prime}})=4-{n_{\circ}}$ ; this yields

$$ \varepsilon_{4,{\chi_{2}}}\mathsf{N}(\mathsf{u}-\mathcal{Q}_{4})_{{\chi_{1}}}=(-1)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+\left(2-(4-{n_{\circ}})\right)2^{{\chi_{1}}-1}\right)=-\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}. $$

Thus the final summand in (4.3) is precisely $(-1)^{{\chi_{2}}}\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}.$ Expanding $\left\lfloor\frac{1}{8}7^{{\chi_{2}}}\right\rceil$ as in Lemma 4.2, we obtain, for ${\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}}>0$ and ${\chi_{3+}}=0$ ,

$$ \mathsf{T}(\mathsf{u})_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},0}=4^{{\chi_{1}}}\frac{1}{8}(7^{{\chi_{2}}}-(-1)^{{\chi_{2}}})+(-1)^{{\chi_{2}}}\frac{1}{8}4^{{\chi_{1}}}+(2-{n_{\circ}})2^{{\chi_{1}}-2}, $$

as required. ∎

By Theorem 3.2, the $\mathrm{O}(q)$ orbits in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ are in bijection with

$$ P_{\lambda,q}:=\{\mathsf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\lambda}\mid\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q}\}. $$

Therefore rephrasing Theorem 4.3 gives the desired result.

#### Corollary 4.4.

Let $q$ be a nondegenerate quadratic form on an $n$ -dimensional space $V$ and let $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ . Denote by $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}$ the corresponding algebraic nilpotent adjoint orbit of $\mathbf{O}(q)$ . Write $\chi_{i}$ for the number of odd parts of multiplicity exactly $i$ in $\lambda$ and ${\chi_{3+}}:=\sum_{i=3}^{n}\chi_{i}$ . Then the number of $\mathrm{O}(q)$ -orbits in $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}(k)$ is $|P_{\lambda,q}|=\mathsf{T}(\overline{q})_{{\chi_{1}},{\chi_{2}},{\chi_{3+}}}.$

Finally, let us formulate an algorithm, suggested by the proofs above, for enumerating the elements of the set $P_{\lambda,q}$ . Set ${n_{\circ}}=\dim(\overline{q})$ and $n=\deg(q)$ .

#### Algorithm 4.5.

Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ . Write $m_{j}$ for the multiplicity of part $j$ in $\lambda$ , and let $D$ be the set of odd parts in $\lambda$ . Set $m=\sum_{j\in D}m_{j}$ .

If $m<{n_{\circ}}$ then $P_{\lambda,q}=\emptyset$ . If $m=0$ and ${n_{\circ}}=0$ then $P_{\lambda,\mathcal{H}}=\{\mathcal{H}\}$ . Otherwise:

Define a subset $E$ of $D$ as follows. If there is at least one part $j\in D$ with $m_{j}\geq 3$ , let $E=\{j\}$ . If $m<4$ then let $E=D$ . Otherwise, choose $E$ to satisfy $\sum_{j\in E}m_{j}=3$ if ${n_{\circ}}$ is odd and $\sum_{j\in E}m_{j}=4$ if ${n_{\circ}}$ is even.

Generate the set $S$ of all tuples $[q_{j}\mid j\in D\setminus E]$ and the (small) set $T$ of all tuples $[q_{j}\mid j\in E]$ (with $\deg(q_{j})=m_{j}$ for each $j$ ).

By construction, for each $\mathsf{q}_{S}\in S$ , there exist one or more tuples $\mathsf{q}_{T}\in T$ such that $\overline{\mathsf{q}_{S}}+\overline{\mathsf{q}_{T}}=\overline{q}$ ; include each of the resulting tuples $[\mathsf{q}_{S},\mathsf{q}_{T}]$ in $P_{\lambda,q}$ .

In particular, $\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}$ has no $k$ -rational points in $\mathfrak{so}(q)$ if and only if $m<{n_{\circ}}$ .

## 5. Representatives for nilpotent orbits

In this section, we show how to generate from an element of $\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ (or $\mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)$ ) an explicit representative of the corresponding rational nilpotent orbit of $G=\mathrm{O}(q)$ (or $G=\mathrm{SO}(q)$ ) on $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{so}(q)$ . We set our notation for $\mathfrak{g}$ and for irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules in Section 5.1. We present the strategy for the algorithm in Section 5.2, and provide the steps in Sections 5.3 to 5.9.

### 5.1. Bases for $\mathfrak{g}$ and for $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules

Suppose $q\cong\mathcal{H}^{\oplus m}\oplus q_{\circ}$ where the anisotropic kernel $q_{\circ}$ is represented by $\langle r_{1},r_{2},\ldots,r_{n_{\circ}}\rangle$ ; then $\dim(V)=n=2m+{n_{\circ}}$ . Let $\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{m},w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}\}$ be a Witt basis of $\mathcal{H}^{\oplus m}$ , that is, with $B_{q}(v_{i},w_{j})=\delta_{i,j}$ , such that the subspace generated by the $v_{i}$ s (respectively, the $w_{i}$ s) is totally isotropic. Complete this to a basis of $V$ by choosing, for $1\leq\kappa,\ell\leq{n_{\circ}}$ , vectors $z_{\ell}$ in the orthogonal complement such that $B_{q}(z_{\ell},z_{\kappa})=\delta_{\ell,\kappa}r_{\ell}$ . Then with respect to the ordered basis $B=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{m},w_{1},\ldots,w_{m},z_{1},\ldots,z_{{n_{\circ}}}\}$ of $V$ , and the corresponding dual basis $B^{*}=\{v_{1}^{*},\ldots,v_{m}^{*},w_{1}^{*},\ldots,w_{m}^{*},z_{1}^{*},\ldots,z_{n_{\circ}}^{*}\}$ of $V^{*}$ , the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}\subset\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ has a maximal split toral subalgebra $\mathfrak{t}$ spanned by

$$ \mathsf{H}_{i}=v_{i}v_{i}^{*}-w_{i}w_{i}^{*},\quad\text{for\>}1\leq i\leq m. $$

Then its centralizer $\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{t}}=\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{s}$ , where $\mathfrak{s}\cong\mathfrak{so}(q_{\circ})$ is spanned by $\{r_{\kappa}z_{\ell}z_{\kappa}^{*}-r_{\ell}z_{\kappa}z_{\ell}^{*}\mid 1\leq\ell<\kappa\leq{n_{\circ}}\}$ . Denoting by $\varepsilon_{i}\in\mathfrak{t}^{*}$ the functional $\varepsilon_{i}(\mathsf{H}_{j})=\delta_{i,j}$ , for each $1\leq i,j\leq m$ , the positive roots of $\mathfrak{g}$ with respect to $\mathfrak{t}$ are $\Phi^{+}=\{\varepsilon_{i}\pm\varepsilon_{j},\varepsilon_{k}\mid 1\leq i<j\leq m,1\leq k\leq m\}$ and the root system is $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup(-\Phi^{+})$ . A basis for each root space is given as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j} \displaystyle\ (1\leq i\neq j\leq m): \displaystyle\mathsf{X}_{i,j} \displaystyle=v_{i}v_{j}^{*}-w_{j}w_{i}^{*} \displaystyle\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j} \displaystyle\ (1\leq i<j\leq m): \displaystyle\mathsf{X}_{i,-j} \displaystyle=v_{i}w_{j}^{*}-v_{j}w_{i}^{*} \displaystyle-\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j} \displaystyle\ (1\leq i<j\leq m): \displaystyle\mathsf{X}_{-i,j} \displaystyle=w_{j}v_{i}^{*}-w_{i}v_{j}^{*} \displaystyle\varepsilon_{i} \displaystyle\ (1\leq i\leq m): \displaystyle\{\mathsf{X}_{i}^{\ell} \displaystyle=z_{\ell}w_{i}^{*}-r_{\ell}v_{i}z_{\ell}^{*}\mid 1\leq\ell\leq{n_{\circ}}\} \displaystyle-\varepsilon_{i} \displaystyle\ (1\leq i\leq m): \displaystyle\{\mathsf{X}_{-i}^{\ell} \displaystyle=z_{\ell}v_{i}^{*}-r_{\ell}w_{i}z_{\ell}^{*}\mid 1\leq\ell\leq{n_{\circ}}\}. $$

With respect to these choices, we have the expected relations $[\mathsf{X}_{i,j},\mathsf{X}_{j,i}]=\mathsf{H}_{i}-\mathsf{H}_{j}$ , $[\mathsf{X}_{i,-j},\mathsf{X}_{-i,j}]=\mathsf{H}_{i}+\mathsf{H}_{j}$ , $[\mathsf{X}_{i}^{\ell},\mathsf{X}_{-i}^{\kappa}]=\delta_{\ell,\kappa}r_{\ell}\mathsf{H}_{i}$ , and also for $i<j$

$$ [\mathsf{X}_{i}^{\ell},\mathsf{X}_{j}^{\kappa}]=-r_{\ell}\delta_{\ell,\kappa}\mathsf{X}_{i,-j},\quad[\mathsf{X}_{-i}^{\ell},\mathsf{X}_{-j}^{\kappa}]=r_{\ell}\delta_{\ell,\kappa}\mathsf{X}_{-i,j},\quad[\mathsf{X}_{i}^{\ell},\mathsf{X}_{-j}^{\ell}]=r_{\ell}\mathsf{X}_{i,j}, $$

whereas if $\ell\neq\kappa$ and $i\neq j$ we have $[\mathsf{X}_{i}^{\ell},\mathsf{X}_{j}^{\kappa}]\in\mathfrak{s}$ .

Suppose now ${\mathrm{d}\phi}=\{Y,H,X\}\subset\mathfrak{so}(q)$ is a Lie triple. Let $U_{i}$ be an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -submodule of $V$ . Then a basis for $U_{i}$ is given by $\{X^{i-1}v,X^{i-2}v,\ldots,Xv,v\}$ , where $v\in U_{i}$ is a lowest weight vector; we’ll call such an ordered basis an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -basis. With respect to this basis, the action of $X$ is given in matrix form as a Jordan block $J_{i}$ , that is, an upper triangular matrix with 1s on the second diagonal and 0s elsewhere. In fact, $H,X,Y$ act by, respectively, the matrices

$$ h_{i}=\textrm{diag}(i-1,i-3,\cdots,-i+3,-i+1),\quad x_{i}=J_{i},\quad\text{and}\quad y_{i}=D_{i}\;{{}^{t}J_{i}} $$

where $D_{i}=\textrm{diag}(0,\mu_{1},\cdots,\mu_{i-1})$ with $\mu_{k}=k(i-k)$ for $1\leq k<i$ . Importantly, by our hypotheses on $p$ we have that the residual characteristic satisfies $p>h$ (where the Coxeter number $h$ of $G$ is $h=2n$ if $n$ is odd, and $h=2(n-1)$ if $n$ is even) so that $\mu_{k}\in\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ , regardless of $i$ . We use this property at various points, whose importance will be evident in Section 7; its necessity for the DeBacker correspondence was discussed in [19].

We want to describe various $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -submodules with respect to the basis $B$ of $V$ in order to construct our desired matrix representatives. In Sections 5.3 to 5.9 we generally do so in one of two ways.

In the first way, given a consecutive subset of the Witt basis, which we take without loss of generality to be $B^{\prime}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i},w_{1},\ldots,w_{i}\}$ , we realize its span $V^{\prime}$ as two copies of $U_{i}$ by choosing the $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -bases $B_{1}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i}\}$ and $B_{2}=\{-w_{i},w_{i-1},\ldots,(-1)^{i}w_{1}\}$ . Then the restriction of ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ to $V^{\prime}$ is given in matrix form by

$$ H|_{V^{\prime}}=\textrm{diag}(h_{i},-h_{i}),\quad X|_{V^{\prime}}=\left[\begin{matrix}x_{i}&0\\
0&-{}^{t}x_{i}\end{matrix}\right],\quad\text{and}\quad Y|_{V^{\prime}}=\left[\begin{matrix}y_{i}&0\\
0&-{}^{t}y_{i}\end{matrix}\right]. $$

Alternatively, if $i=2k+1$ is odd, we may take a consecutive subset such as $B_{k}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k},w_{1},\ldots,w_{k}\}$ of the Witt basis, together with a vector $x$ in the span of $B\setminus B_{k}$ (which is not necessarily in $\mathrm{span}\{z_{1},\cdots,z_{{n_{\circ}}}\}$ !) satisfying $q(x)=r$ , which will take the role of the 0-weight vector of the module. Then

$$ B^{\prime}=\{rv_{1},rv_{2},\ldots,rv_{k},x,-w_{k},w_{k-1},\ldots,(-1)^{k}w_{1}\} $$

is an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -basis of a submodule $V^{\prime}$ isomorphic to $U_{i}$ , such that $q|_{V^{\prime}}\cong\langle r\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus k}\cong\langle r\rangle\otimes(\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus k})$ . The restriction of ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ to $V^{\prime}$ is given in matrix form relative to the ordered basis $B_{k}\cup\{x\}$ by

$$ \displaystyle H|_{V^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\textrm{diag}(\tilde{h}_{k},-\tilde{h}_{k},0),\quad\text{where}\quad\tilde{h}_{k}=\textrm{diag}(2k,2k-2,\cdots,2), \displaystyle X|_{V^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\left[\begin{matrix}x_{k}&0&M_{r}\\
0&-{}^{t}x_{k}&0\\
0&{}^{t}M_{1}&0\end{matrix}\right],\quad\text{and}\quad Y|_{V^{\prime}}=\left[\begin{matrix}\tilde{y}_{k}&0&0\\
0&-{}^{t}\tilde{y}_{k}&M_{-1}\\
{}^{t}M_{r^{-1}}&0&0\end{matrix}\right], $$

where $M_{s}$ denotes the $k\times 1$ matrix $(\delta_{i,k}s)_{1\leq i\leq k}$ , and $\tilde{y}_{k}$ is the $k$ th order principal submatrix of $y_{i}$ . We make the convention that if $k=0$ then $\tilde{h}_{0}$ is omitted.

### 5.2. The strategy

Now suppose that $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})\in\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ or $\mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)$ , so that $\lambda\in\Lambda^{e}(n)$ and $\mathsf{q}=[q_{i_{1}},\cdots,q_{i_{s}}]\in P_{\lambda,q}$ (or is taken to be $\mathcal{H}$ if $\lambda$ has no odd parts). Let $m_{i}$ be the multiplicity of $i$ in $\lambda$ . Thus each distinct part in $\lambda$ corresponds to an orthogonal component of the direct sum (3.2), on which the restriction of $q$ is equivalent to $q_{i_{k}}$ if the part $i_{k}$ is odd, or else to a direct sum of hyperbolic planes if the part is even. When $-1\notin k^{2}$ , some complications may arise, as in the following example.

#### Example 1.

Suppose $\lambda=(1,3,5)$ and $q=\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus 4}$ . If $-1\in k^{2}$ , then $P_{\lambda,q}=\{[1,a,-a],[a,1,-a],[a,-a,1]\mid a\in\{\pm 1,\pm\varpi\}\}$ (writing $a$ in place of $\langle a\rangle$ ) which has $\mathsf{N}(q)_{3}=10$ distinct elements. To $[1,\varpi,-\varpi]\in P_{\lambda,q}$ , for example, one associates a decomposition $V=V_{1}\oplus V_{3}\oplus V_{5}$ with quadratic forms $q_{1}=\langle 1\rangle$ , $q_{3}=\langle\varpi\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}$ and $q_{5}=\langle-\varpi\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus 2}$ , respectively. Thus $V_{3}\oplus V_{5}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of hyperbolic planes (though individually neither one is), and $(q_{1},V_{1})\simeq(q,V)$ . On the other hand, however, now suppose $-1\notin k^{2}$ . Then to $\mathsf{q}=[\rho,\rho,\rho]\in P_{\lambda,q}$ we associate a decomposition as above but in this case, no single $V_{i}$ carries a form equivalent to $q$ !

As this example illustrates, the difficulty is that although $q\simeq q_{i_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus q_{i_{s}}$ , it is not in general true that one can partition the basis $B$ to reflect this orthogonal decomposition, and thus choices of embeddings of $(q_{i},V_{i})$ into $(q,V)$ must be made. An optimal choice, as will be discussed in Section 7, is one for which the span of the roots on whose spaces $X$ and $Y$ are supported has the smallest dimension. We proceed as follows.

We set some notation. Recall that we have fixed a diagonal representative $\langle r_{1},\ldots,r_{n_{\circ}}\rangle$ for $q_{\circ}$ . Let $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})\in\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ or $\mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)$ . Let

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\lambda}=\{(i,j)\mid\text{$i\in\lambda$, $1\leq j\leq m_{i}$}\} $$

be the set of all index pairs, which has cardinality $|\lambda|=\sum_{i\in\lambda}m_{i}$ , the number of parts in $\lambda$ . Write $\mathsf{q}=[q_{j_{1}},\ldots,q_{j_{s}}]$ and for each odd part $i=j_{t}$ ( $1\leq t\leq s)$ of $\lambda$ let $q_{i}\simeq\langle r_{i,1},r_{i,2},\ldots,r_{i,m_{i}}\rangle$ be a diagonal form of $q_{i}$ . This defines a choice of map $(i,j)\mapsto r_{i,j}$ on all $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ such that $i$ is odd.

#### Proposition 5.1.

There exists a partition $\Gamma$ of $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ into subsets of the form:

$\{(i,j),(i,j+1)\}$ such that $i$ is even;

$\{(i,j),(i,j^{\prime})\}$ such that $i$ is odd, $j\neq j^{\prime}$ and $\langle r_{i,j}\rangle\cong\langle-r_{i,j^{\prime}}\rangle$ ;

$\{(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\}$ such that $i\neq i^{\prime}$ are odd, and $\langle r_{i,j}\rangle\cong\langle-r_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}\rangle$ ;

if $-1\notin k^{2}$ : $\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2}),(i_{3},j_{3}),(i_{4},j_{4})\}$ such that the $i_{k}$ are distinct odd parts and $\langle r_{i_{1},j_{1}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{2},j_{2}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{3},j_{3}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{4},j_{4}}\rangle$ ;

if $-1\notin k^{2}$ , $\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2}),(i_{3},j_{3})\}$ such that the $i_{k}$ are distinct odd parts, and there exists $1\leq\ell\leq{n_{\circ}}$ such that $\langle-r_{\ell}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{1},j_{1}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{2},j_{2}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i_{3},j_{3}}\rangle$ ;

if $-1\notin k^{2}$ , $\{(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\}$ such that $i\neq i^{\prime}$ are odd and there exist $1\leq\kappa<\ell\leq{n_{\circ}}$ such that $\langle r_{i,j}\rangle\cong\langle r_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}\rangle\cong\langle-r_{\kappa}\rangle\cong\langle-r_{\ell}\rangle$ ;

for some $t\leq{n_{\circ}}$ : $\{(i_{s},j_{s})\mid 1\leq s\leq t\}$ such that up to permutation of the diagonal representative of $q_{\circ}$ we have $\langle r_{i_{s},j_{s}}\rangle\cong\langle r_{s}\rangle$ for each $1\leq s\leq t$ ;

and such that there are in total at most two sets of the form trip, sign or ani in $\Gamma$ .

#### Proof.

Even parts occur with even multiplicity, so the index pairs $(i,j)$ with $i$ even can be partitioned into couples of the form even. Thus it suffices to consider the case that all parts $i$ of $\lambda$ are odd.

If $-1\in k^{2}$ , then $\langle r\rangle=\langle-r\rangle$ so exhaustively matching up elements of $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ using hyp or pairs leaves at most four index pairs $(i,j)$ , such that each $r_{i,j}$ represents a distinct square class in $\{1,\rho,\varpi,\rho\varpi\}$ . Since $\overline{\mathsf{q}}=\overline{q}$ , we deduce these must satisfy ani. Therefore the lemma holds in this case.

If $-1\notin k^{2}$ , then exhaustively matching up elements using hyp or pairs leaves at most two sets of index pairs: $S_{a}$ and $S_{\varpi b}$ , consisting of those $(i,j)$ for which $\langle r_{i,j}\rangle\cong\langle a\rangle$ or $\langle r_{i,j}\rangle\cong\langle\varpi b\rangle$ , for some fixed $a,b\in\{1,\rho\}$ , respectively. We claim that $S_{a}$ and $S_{\varpi b}$ can each be partitioned as required, with at most one part of the form trip, sign or ani.

If $S_{a}\cup S_{\varpi b}$ satisfies ani, we are done. If not, then given the classification of Table 1, there is at least one $r\in\{a,\varpi b\}$ such that $|S_{r}|>2$ ; we now consider each such $r$ in turn.

If $S_{r}$ contains two distinct elements $(i,j)$ and $(i,j^{\prime})$ with the same part $i$ of $\lambda$ , then by applying the relation $\langle r,r\rangle\cong\langle-r,-r\rangle$ , we can replace the diagonal form of the corresponding $q_{i}$ with one in which $r_{i,j}=r_{i,j^{\prime}}=-r$ instead. Since $|S_{r}|>2$ , we may then apply hyp or pairs, removing at least two (and perhaps four) elements from $S_{r}$ . Repeat this process until either: the resulting $S_{r}$ has two or fewer elements, in which case ani applies and we are done; or all the parts $i$ of $\lambda$ occuring in elements of the resulting $S_{r}$ are distinct. In the latter case, we next exhaustively eliminate quadruples from $S_{r}$ using quad, leaving at most three elements. Recalling that $\langle r,r,r\rangle\simeq\langle-r\rangle$ and $\langle r,r\rangle\cong\langle-r,-r\rangle$ , we conclude that exactly one of trip, sign or ani must apply to what is left of $S_{r}$ , and we are done. ∎

Choose such a partition $\Gamma$ . For each $\textsf{{L}}\in\{{\textsf{{even}}},{\textsf{{hyp}}},{\textsf{{pairs}}},{\textsf{{quad}}},{\textsf{{trip}}},{\textsf{{sign}}},{\textsf{{ani}}}\}$ , let $\Gamma_{\textsf{{L}}}$ denote the set of parts of $\Gamma$ falling under case L. For each $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{trip}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{sign}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{ani}}}$ , if any, we have that $\oplus_{(i,j)\in\gamma}\langle r_{i,j}\rangle$ represents a nontrivial element of the Witt group, and these are the only such parts in $\Gamma$ .

In the following sections we partition the basis $B$ according to $\Gamma$ , giving an orthogonal decomposition $V=\oplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma}V_{\gamma}$ . On each orthogonal subspace $V_{\gamma}$ we construct an action of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ such that their direct sum is isomorphic to a decomposition (3.2) associated to $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})$ . In doing so, we define a Lie triple ${\mathrm{d}\phi}=\{Y,H,X\}$ such that $X$ represents the nilpotent orbit corresponding to $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})$ . Since $X$ is a sum of its restrictions to each $V_{\gamma}$ , and each $V_{\gamma}$ is spanned by a subset of $B$ , we will recoup an expression for $X$ as a linear combination of root vectors, and thus an explicit representative of the orbit.

For ease of notation, in each case we suppose the subset $B_{\gamma}$ of $B$ starts with $\{v_{1},w_{1}\}$ ; to implement this algorithm in practice, one chooses an appropriate partition of $B$ and shifts the indices on all the vectors and root vectors.

### 5.3. $\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}$ : even parts of $\lambda$ , and $\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$ : hyperbolic planes in odd parts of $\lambda$

Suppose $\gamma=\{(i,j),(i,j^{\prime})\}\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$ . Then $V_{\gamma}$ should be a sum of two copies of $U_{i}$ and the restriction of $q$ to $V_{\gamma}$ should be a split quadratic space of dimension $2i$ . Therefore we choose a consecutive subset of the Witt basis with $2i$ elements, which up to relabeling we may take to be $B_{\gamma}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i},w_{1},\ldots,w_{i}\}$ . Set $V_{\gamma}=\mathrm{span}(B_{\gamma})$ and define an action of ${\mathrm{d}\phi}$ as in (5.3). Then $V_{\gamma}\cong U_{i}\oplus U_{i}$ and the restriction of $q$ to $V_{\gamma}$ is isometric to $\mathcal{H}^{\oplus i}$ . From the matrix form we deduce that $X|_{V_{\gamma}}$ is a sum of simple root vectors. Specifically, we have

$$ X|_{V_{\gamma}}=\sum_{1\leq t<i}\mathsf{X}_{t,t+1},\quad\text{and}\quad Y|_{V_{\gamma}}=\sum_{1\leq t<i}\mu_{t}\mathsf{X}_{t+1,t}, $$

where we note that $Y|_{V_{\gamma}}$ is a linear combination of exactly the corresponding negative root vectors.

By choosing disjoint subsets $B_{\gamma}$ for each $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$ , we thus create an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -submodule $V_{{\textsf{{hyp}}}}=\oplus V_{\gamma}$ of $V$ .

### 5.4. $\Gamma_{\textsf{{pairs}}}$ : Hyperbolic planes across two distinct odd parts

Suppose now that $\gamma=\{(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\}\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{pairs}}}$ . Scaling by a square if necessary, we may assume that $r_{i,j}=r$ and $r_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}=-r$ for some $r$ . Write $i=2k+1$ , $i^{\prime}=2k^{\prime}+1$ , with $k>k^{\prime}\geq 0$ , and set $p=\frac{1}{2}(i+i^{\prime})=k+k^{\prime}+1$ .

Here, $V_{\gamma}$ should be isomorphic to $U_{i}\oplus U_{i^{\prime}}$ as $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules, and the restriction of $q$ to $V_{\gamma}$ should be $(\langle r\rangle\otimes(\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus k}))\oplus(\langle-r\rangle\otimes(\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus k^{\prime}}))\cong\mathcal{H}^{\oplus 2p}$ . We use the relation

$$ {}^{t}K\left[\begin{matrix}0&1\\
1&0\end{matrix}\right]K=\left[\begin{matrix}r&0\\
0&-r\end{matrix}\right],\quad\text{with}\;K=\left[\begin{matrix}r/2&r/2\\
1&-1\end{matrix}\right], $$

to explicitly identify the two-dimensional 0-weight space, which carries the form $\langle r,-r\rangle$ , with a hyperbolic plane $\mathcal{H}$ spanned by a Witt basis.

That is, choose a subset of the Witt basis with $2p$ elements, which up to relabeling we take to be $B_{\gamma}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{p},w_{1},\ldots,w_{p}\}$ . Identify the 2-dimensional 0-weight space with the span of $\{v_{p},w_{p}\}$ by choosing $x^{\pm}_{p}=\frac{r}{2}v_{p}\pm w_{p}$ as our $0$ -weight vectors. Note that $q(x^{\pm}_{p})=\pm r$ . Then $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -bases for the corresponding decomposition of $B_{\gamma}$ into orthogonal $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k)$ -invariant subspaces are

$$ B_{i}=\{rv_{1},rv_{2},\ldots,rv_{k},x_{p}^{+},-w_{k},w_{k-1},\ldots,(-1)^{k}w_{1}\} $$

and

$$ B_{i^{\prime}}=\{rv_{k+1},rv_{k+2},\ldots,rv_{k+k^{\prime}},x^{-}_{p},w_{k+k^{\prime}},-w_{k+k^{\prime}-1},\ldots,(-1)^{k^{\prime}+1}w_{k+1}\}, $$

respectively, giving the required $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -structure to $V_{\gamma}=\mathrm{span}{(B_{\gamma})}$ .

We next write down explicit representatives of the restrictions of $H$ and of $X$ to $V_{\gamma}$ with respect to $B_{\gamma}$ , which amounts to performing a change of coordinates from $B_{i}\cup B_{i^{\prime}}$ , with respect to which these matrices are given as in (5.2).

We have $H|_{V_{\gamma}}=\textrm{diag}(\tilde{h}_{k},\tilde{h}_{k^{\prime}},0,-\tilde{h}_{k},-\tilde{h}_{k^{\prime}},0)$ . If $k^{\prime}=0$ then it follows from the bases above that $Xv_{1}=0$ , $Xv_{p}=v_{k}$ , and $Xv_{i}=v_{i-1}$ for $1<i<p$ , whereas if $k^{\prime}>0$ then instead $Xv_{k+1}=0$ and $Xv_{p}=v_{k}+v_{k+k^{\prime}}$ . Similarly, if $k^{\prime}=0$ we have $Xw_{p}=\frac{r}{2}v_{k}$ , $Xw_{k}=-\frac{r}{2}v_{p}-w_{p}$ and $Xw_{i}=-w_{i+1}$ for all $1\leq i<k$ , whereas if $k^{\prime}>0$ then instead $Xw_{p}=\frac{r}{2}v_{k}-\frac{r}{2}v_{k+k^{\prime}}$ and $Xw_{k+k^{\prime}}=\frac{r}{2}v_{p}-w_{p}$ . Using the notation of (5.1), we may thus write the restriction of $X$ to $V_{\gamma}$ as the sum of positive root vectors

$$ X|_{V_{\gamma}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k+k^{\prime}\\
j\neq k\end{subarray}}\mathsf{X}_{j,j+1}+\mathsf{X}_{k,p}+\frac{r}{2}\mathsf{X}_{k,-p}+\mathsf{X}_{k+k^{\prime},p}-\frac{r}{2}\mathsf{X}_{k+k^{\prime},-p} $$

where if $k^{\prime}=0$ we omit the two terms in which $k+k^{\prime}$ appears as a subscript. Similarly, $Y|_{V_{\gamma}}$ is a linear combination (with coefficients in $\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ ) of the root vectors

$$ \{\mathsf{X}_{j+1,j},\mathsf{X}_{p,k},r^{-1}\mathsf{X}_{-k,p},(\mathsf{X}_{p,k+k^{\prime}}),(r^{-1}\mathsf{X}_{-p,k+k^{\prime}})\mid 1\leq j<k+k^{\prime},j\neq k\}, $$

omitting the terms in parentheses when $k^{\prime}=0$ .

Making suitable choices of disjoint bases $B_{\gamma}$ , for each $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{pairs}}}$ , yields another split quadratic subspace $V_{{\textsf{{pairs}}}}=\oplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{pairs}}}}V_{\gamma}\subseteq V$ .

### 5.5. $\Gamma_{{\textsf{{quad}}}}$ : Hyperbolic planes across four parts, when $-1\notin k^{2}$

Suppose now that

$$ \gamma=\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2}),(i_{3},j_{3}),(i_{4},j_{4})\}\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{quad}}} $$

with $i_{1}>i_{2}>i_{3}>i_{4}$ , and after scaling by squares if necessary, let $r$ be the common value of $r_{i_{t},j_{t}}$ for $1\leq t\leq 4$ . Let $i_{t}=2k_{t}+1$ for each $t$ , and set $p=\frac{1}{2}\sum i_{t}=k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4}+2$ . Choose a subset of the Witt basis with $2p$ elements, which we assume up to relabelling is $B_{\gamma}=\{v_{1},\cdots,v_{p},w_{1},\cdots,w_{p}\}.$ This space is to carry the module $\oplus_{t}U_{i_{t}}$ with form $\langle r,r,r,r\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus p-2}$ . We choose its hyperbolic four dimensional $0$ -weight space to coincide with $W_{0}=\mathrm{span}\{v_{p-1},v_{p},w_{p-1},w_{p}\}$ . Using the change of basis matrix $K$ from (5.6) we diagonalize $B_{q}$ on this subspace to $\textrm{diag}(r,r,-r,-r)$ . Next, since $-1\notin k^{2}$ , there exist $c,s\in k^{\times}$ such that $c^{2}+s^{2}=-1$ . A matrix $C$ satisfying ${}^{t}C(-rI)C=rI$ is given by

$$ C=\left[\begin{matrix}c&-s\\
s&c\end{matrix}\right]. $$

Consequently, the following vectors form an orthogonal basis of $W_{0}$ in which each vector $x_{t}$ satisfies $q(x_{t})=r$ :

$$ \displaystyle x_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{r}{2}v_{p-1}+w_{p-1},\quad \displaystyle x_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{r}{2}v_{p}+w_{p}, \displaystyle x_{3} \displaystyle=\frac{cr}{2}v_{p-1}+\frac{sr}{2}v_{p}-cw_{p-1}-sw_{p}, \displaystyle x_{4} \displaystyle=\frac{-sr}{2}v_{p-1}+\frac{cr}{2}v_{p}+sw_{p-1}-cw_{p}. $$

We complete each of these to an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -basis of $U_{i_{t}}$ , respectively, by partitioning the remaining elements of $B_{\gamma}$ as before. Specifically, setting $p_{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}k_{s}$ , so that $p_{0}=0$ and $p_{4}=p-2$ , ordered bases of the four $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ submodules are

$$ B_{t}=\{rv_{p_{t-1}+1},rv_{p_{t-1}+2},\cdots,rv_{p_{t}},x_{t},-w_{p_{t}},\cdots,(-1)^{k_{t}}w_{p_{t-1}+1}\}, $$

where it is understood that if $k_{4}=0$ then $B_{4}=\{x_{4}\}$ , a one-dimensional space.

These bases define the restriction of the Lie triple $\{Y,H,X\}$ to $V_{\gamma}=\mathrm{span}(B_{\gamma})$ . For example, the matrix of $H_{V_{\gamma}}$ is

$$ \textrm{diag}(\tilde{h}_{k_{1}},\tilde{h}_{k_{2}},\tilde{h}_{k_{3}},\tilde{h}_{k_{4}},0,0,-\tilde{h}_{k_{1}},-\tilde{h}_{k_{2}},-\tilde{h}_{k_{3}},-\tilde{h}_{k_{4}},0,0). $$

To obtain the matrix of the restriction of $X$ to $V_{\gamma}$ with respect to $B_{\gamma}$ , we first invert (5.10), and then apply the relations $Xx_{i}=rv_{p_{i}}$ to deduce

$$ \displaystyle Xv_{p-1}=v_{p_{1}}-cv_{p_{3}}+sv_{p_{4}} \displaystyle Xv_{p}=v_{p_{2}}-sv_{p_{3}}-cv_{p_{4}} \displaystyle Xw_{p-1}=\frac{r}{2}v_{p_{1}}+\frac{cr}{2}v_{p_{3}}-\frac{sr}{2}v_{p_{4}} \displaystyle Xw_{p}=\frac{r}{2}v_{p_{2}}+\frac{sr}{2}v_{p_{3}}+\frac{cr}{2}v_{p_{4}}, $$

where if $k_{4}=0$ we omit the four terms containing the subscript $p_{4}$ . The action of $X$ on the remaining $v_{i}$ and $w_{i}$ of $B_{\gamma}$ can be read from the bases (5.11) directly, and contribute sums of simple root vectors as before. With respect to the root vectors (5.1), the restriction of $X$ to $V_{\gamma}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle X|_{V_{\gamma}}=\sum_{1\leq j<p-2,j\neq p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}} \displaystyle\mathsf{X}_{j,j+1}+\mathsf{X}_{p_{1},p-1}+\mathsf{X}_{p_{2},p}-c\mathsf{X}_{p_{3},p-1}-s\mathsf{X}_{p_{3},p} \displaystyle+\frac{r}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{1},-(p-1)}+\frac{r}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{2},-p}+\frac{cr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{3},-(p-1)}+\frac{sr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{3},-p} \displaystyle+s\mathsf{X}_{p_{4},p-1}-c\mathsf{X}_{p_{4},p}+\frac{-sr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{4},-(p-1)}+\frac{cr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p_{4},-p}, $$

where the four terms containing $p_{4}$ as a subscript are omitted if $k_{4}=0$ . As before, one can verify that $Y|_{V_{\gamma}}$ is a linear combination of the corresponding negative root vectors, with the proviso that if a root vector appears with coefficient in $a\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ in (5.12) for some $a\in k$ then the corresponding negative root vector appears with a coefficient in $a^{-1}\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ in $Y|_{V_{\gamma}}$ , that is, with the negative valuation.

Choosing disjoint subsets $B_{\gamma}$ , for each $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{quad}}}$ , gives an $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -invariant split quadratic subspace $V_{{\textsf{{quad}}}}=\oplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{quad}}}}V_{\gamma}$ of $V$ .

### 5.6. $\Gamma_{\textsf{{trip}}}$ : Anisotropic part, when $-1\notin k^{2}$ and a triple identity is required

Suppose $-1\notin k^{2}$ and $\gamma=\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2}),(i_{3},j_{3})\}\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{trip}}}$ ; without loss of generality we assume $i_{1}>i_{2}>i_{3}$ and $r_{i_{1},j_{1}}=r_{i_{2},j_{2}}=r_{i_{3},j_{3}}=-r$ . Let $\ell\in\{1,\ldots,{n_{\circ}}\}$ be such that $r=r_{\ell}$ ; then by the proof of Proposition 5.1 we know that this is the only occurrence of $r$ (up to scaling by $(k^{\times})^{2}$ ) in the diagonal form of $q_{\circ}$ . Let $k_{t}=(i_{t}-1)/2$ for each $t$ and set $p=k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}+1$ . In this case, $V_{\gamma}$ should be isomorphic to $U_{i_{1}}\oplus U_{i_{2}}\oplus U_{i_{3}}$ and carry the form $\langle-r,-r,-r\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus p-1}\cong\langle r\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus p}$ . Therefore, up to relabeling of the Witt basis, we choose the subset

$$ B_{\gamma}=\{v_{1},\cdots,v_{p},w_{1},\cdots,w_{p},z_{\ell}\}. $$

The restriction of $q$ to $W_{0}=\mathrm{span}\{v_{p},w_{p},z_{\ell}\}$ can be transformed to the diagonal form $\langle-r,-r,-r\rangle$ by first applying the matrix $K$ of (5.6) to the first two coordinates, then $C$ of (5.9) to the first and last coordinates. Thus the orthogonal vectors

$$ x_{1}=\frac{cr}{2}v_{p}+cw_{p}+sz_{\ell},\quad x_{2}=\frac{r}{2}v_{p}-w_{p},\quad\text{and}\quad x_{3}=-\frac{sr}{2}v_{p}-sw_{p}+cz_{\ell} $$

each satisfy $q(x_{i})=-r$ , which implies that the following bases span complementary quadratic subspaces of $V_{\gamma}=\mathrm{span}(B_{\gamma})$ , each with anisotropic kernel $\langle-r\rangle$ :

$$ \displaystyle B_{1}=\{-rv_{1},\ldots,-rv_{k_{1}},x_{1},-w_{k_{1}},\ldots,(-1)^{k_{1}}w_{1}\} \displaystyle B_{2}=\{-rv_{k_{1}+1},\ldots,-rv_{k_{1}+k_{2}},x_{2},-w_{k_{1}+k_{2}},\ldots,(-1)^{k_{2}}w_{k_{1}+1}\} \displaystyle B_{3}=\{-rv_{k_{1}+k_{2}+1},\ldots,-rv_{k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}},x_{3},-w_{k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}},\ldots,(-1)^{k_{3}}w_{k_{1}+k_{2}+1}\} $$

where it is understood that $B_{3}=\{x_{3}\}$ if $k_{3}=0$ . We interpret the $B_{i}$ as standard bases for $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules as usual. With respect to $B_{\gamma}$ the matrix of the restriction of $H$ to $V_{\gamma}$ is $\textrm{diag}(\tilde{h}_{k_{1}},\tilde{h}_{k_{2}},\tilde{h}_{k_{3}},0,-\tilde{h}_{k_{1}},-\tilde{h}_{k_{2}},-\tilde{h}_{k_{3}},0,0)$ . The action of $X$ can be determined from the bases $B_{t}$ above, noting that

$$ v_{p}=-cr^{-1}x_{1}+r^{-1}x_{2}+sr^{-1}x_{3},\quad w_{p}=\frac{1}{2}(-cx_{1}-x_{2}+sx_{3}),\quad z_{\ell}=-sx_{1}-cx_{3}. $$

It follows that in terms of the root vectors (5.1) we have

$$ \displaystyle X|_{V_{\gamma}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<p-1\\
j\neq k_{1},k_{1}+k_{2}\end{subarray}} \displaystyle\mathsf{X}_{j,j+1}+c\mathsf{X}_{k_{1},p}-\mathsf{X}_{k_{1}+k_{2},p}-s\mathsf{X}_{p-1,p}+ \displaystyle+\frac{cr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{k_{1},-p}+\frac{r}{2}\mathsf{X}_{k_{1}+k_{2},-p}-\frac{sr}{2}\mathsf{X}_{p-1,-p}-s\mathsf{X}^{\ell}_{k_{1}}-c\mathsf{X}^{\ell}_{p-1} $$

where if $k_{3}=0$ we omit the three terms having $p-1$ as a subscript. Similarly, we can readily determine that $Y|_{V_{\gamma}}$ is a linear combination (with coefficients in $\mathcal{R}^{\times}$ ) of the root vectors

$$ \displaystyle\{\mathsf{X}_{j+1,j},\mathsf{X}_{p,k_{1}},\mathsf{X}_{p,k_{1}+k_{2}},(\mathsf{X}_{p,p-1}),r^{-1}X_{-k_{1},p},r^{-1}\mathsf{X}_{-(k_{1}+k_{2}),p},(r^{-1}\mathsf{X}_{-(p-1),p}), \displaystyle r^{-1}\mathsf{X}^{\ell}_{-k_{1}},(r^{-1}\mathsf{X}^{\ell}_{p-1})\mid 1\leq j<p-1,j\neq k_{1},j\neq k_{1}+k_{2}\} $$

where the vectors in parentheses are omitted if $k_{3}=0$ .

### 5.7. $\Gamma_{{\textsf{{sign}}}}$ : Anisotropic part, when $-1\notin k^{2}$ and sign change is required

Now suppose $-1\notin k^{2}$ and $\gamma=\{(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\}\in\Gamma_{{\textsf{{sign}}}}$ . We assume without loss of generality that $i>i^{\prime}$ and $r_{i,j}=r_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}=-r$ . By the proof of Proposition 5.1, there are exactly two indices $\ell<\kappa$ in $\{1,\ldots,{n_{\circ}}\}$ such that $r=r_{\ell}=r_{\kappa}$ . Let $k=(i-1)/2$ , $k^{\prime}=(i^{\prime}-1)/2$ and $p=k+k^{\prime}$ . Then $V_{\gamma}$ should be isomorphic to $U_{i}\oplus U_{i^{\prime}}$ as $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules and carry the form $\langle-r,-r\rangle\oplus\mathcal{H}^{\oplus p}$ . Therefore, up to numbering of the Witt basis, we choose the subset

$$ B_{\gamma}=\{v_{1},\cdots,v_{p},w_{1},\cdots,w_{p},z_{\ell},z_{\kappa}\}. $$

The matrix $C$ of (5.9) transforms $\langle r,r\rangle$ to $\langle-r,-r\rangle$ , so the vectors

$$ x_{1}=cz_{\ell}-sz_{\kappa}\quad\text{and}\quad x_{2}=sz_{\ell}+cz_{\kappa} $$

each satisfy $q(x_{i})=-r$ . Thus the following bases span complementary quadratic subspaces of the span $V_{\gamma}$ of $B_{\gamma}$ , each with anisotropic kernel $\langle-r\rangle$ :

$$ \displaystyle B_{1}=\{-rv_{1},\ldots,-rv_{k},x_{1},-w_{k},\ldots,(-1)^{k}w_{1}\} \displaystyle B_{2}=\{-rv_{k+1},\ldots,-rv_{k+k^{\prime}},x_{2},-w_{k+k^{\prime}},\ldots,(-1)^{k^{\prime}}w_{k+1}\} $$

where it is understood that $B_{2}=\{x_{2}\}$ if $k^{\prime}=0$ . We interpret the $B_{i}$ as standard bases for $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(k)$ -modules as usual. With respect to $B_{\gamma}$ the matrix of the restriction of $H$ to $V_{\gamma}$ is $\textrm{diag}(\tilde{h}_{k},\tilde{h}_{k^{\prime}},-\tilde{h}_{k},-\tilde{h}_{k^{\prime}},0,0)$ .
