#### Remark 4.3.

If $u\leq v$ in the Bruhat order, which corresponds to the special case $\mathbf{a}=(1,\dots,1)$ , then the tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ recover the classical Richardson varieties $\mathcal{R}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{u,v}$ , respectively.

The following theorem gives a necessary condition for the nonemptiness of tilted Richardson varieties in terms of the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted Bruhat order $\leq_{\mathbf{a}}$ (see Definition 3.8) and also characterizes their $T$ -fixed points.

#### Theorem 4.4.

For $u,v\in S_{n}$ , if $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}\neq\emptyset$ or $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\neq\emptyset$ , then $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . Furthermore, if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , the set of $T$ -fixed points in $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ corresponds exactly to the elements of the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the first statement only for $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ . The case for $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is similar. Assume, for contradiction, that $u\not\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . By definition, there exist indices $k,i\in[n]$ such that $\#\left\{u[k]\cap[a_{k},i)_{c}\right\}<\#\left\{v[k]\cap[a_{k},i)_{c}\right\}$ , or equivalently,

$$ \#\left\{u[k]\cap[a_{k},i)_{c}\right\}+\#\left\{v[k]\cap[i,a_{k})_{c}\right\}<k. $$

However, if $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ , then the inequality above implies $\rank_{[a_{k},i)_{c}}(F_{k})+\rank_{[i,a_{k})_{c}}(F_{k})<k$ by Definition 4.1. This contradicts with the fact that

$$ \rank_{[a_{k},i)_{c}}(F_{k})+\rank_{[i,a_{k})_{c}}(F_{k})\geq\dim(F_{k})=k. $$

Thus, we must have $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . The second statement follows directly from Theorem 3.13. ∎

In particular, the set of $T$ -fixed points in $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ is independent of the choice of the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ as long as $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . We will later show (Corollary 4.10) that the varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ themselves are independent of the choice of the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ .

### 4.2. Definition via Cyclically Rotated Grassmannian Richardson Varieties

We present an alternative definition of tilted Richardson varieties using intersections of cyclically rotated Richardson varieties in the Grassmannian (Theorem 4.7). Later, we use this alternative definition to show that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ are independent of the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ as long as $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ (Corollary 4.10). We begin by defining these cyclically rotated varieties.

For a subspace $V\in\gr_{k,n}$ , let $M_{V}$ be a $n\times k$ matrix that represents $V$ . Define the cyclic rotation map $\tau:\gr_{k,n}\rightarrow\gr_{k,n}$ by setting

$$ \tau(M_{V}):=\begin{bmatrix}\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{n}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{1}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
&\vdots&\\
\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{n-1}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
\end{bmatrix},\quad\text{where}\quad M_{V}=\begin{bmatrix}\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{1}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{2}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
&\vdots&\\
\text{---}&\hskip-5.69046pt\vec{v}_{n}&\hskip-5.69046pt\text{---}\\
\end{bmatrix}. $$

For an index set $I=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}\subseteq[n]$ , define its cyclic rotation as $\tau(I):=\{i_{1}+1,\dots,i_{k}+1\}$ , where the index $n+1$ is identified with $1$ .

#### Definition 4.5.

For subsets $I,J\subseteq[n]$ with $|I|=|J|$ and $r\in[n]$ such that $I\leq_{r}J$ , define the cyclically rotated (open) Grassmannian Richardson varieties by

$$ \mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,r}:=\tau^{r-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{\tau^{1-r}(I),\tau^{1-r}(J)})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}:=\tau^{r-1}(\mathcal{R}_{\tau^{1-r}(I),\tau^{1-r}(J)}). $$

Cyclically rotated Grassmannian Richardson varieties are special cases of positroid varieties (see [31, Section 6]). Like Grassmannian Richardson varieties, they can also be characterized via vanishing conditions on Plücker coordinates.

#### Proposition 4.6.

Let $I,J\subseteq[n]$ , $r\in[n]$ with $|I|=|J|$ and $I\leq_{r}J$ under the shifted Gale order. Denote by $[I,J]_{r}:=\{K\subseteq[n]:I\leq_{r}K\leq_{r}J\}$ the interval in the shifted Gale order. Then

$$ \mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}=\{V\in\gr_{k,n}:\Delta_{K}(V)=0\text{ for all }K\notin[I,J]_{r}\}. $$

The corresponding open cell is $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,r}=\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}\cap\{\Delta_{I}\Delta_{J}\neq 0\}$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 2.6 and the identity $\tau_{\ast}(\Delta_{K})=\Delta_{\tau(K)}$ , $\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}=\{V\in\gr_{k,n}:\Delta_{\tau^{r-1}(K)}(V)=0\text{ for all }K\notin[\tau^{1-r}(I),\tau^{1-r}(J)]\}$ . The desired statement follows from the fact that $A\leq_{r}B\iff\tau^{1-r}(A)\leq\tau^{1-r}(B)$ . The open case follows from similar arguments. ∎

We now present the alternative definition of tilted Richardson varieties as intersections of preimages of cyclically rotated Richardson varieties under natural projection maps.

#### Theorem 4.7.

Let $\pi_{k}:\fl_{n}\rightarrow\gr_{k,n}$ be the projection map defined by $\pi_{k}(F_{\bullet})=F_{k}$ . For $u,v\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}=\bigcap_{k=1}^{n-1}\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}=\bigcap_{k=1}^{n-1}\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}). $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately by comparing the rank conditions in Definition 4.1 with the rank conditions on Grassmannian Richardson varieties in Section 2.2.4, after applying a cyclic rotation. ∎

Since each $\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})$ is a closed subvariety of $\fl_{n}$ and each $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}$ is open, we obtain the following immediate corollary.

#### Corollary 4.8.

$\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ is a closed subvariety of $\fl_{n}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ is an open subvariety.

Our next goal is to establish that the tilted Richardson varieties are independent of the choice of the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ as long as $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . To do so, we first prove the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.9.

Let $I,J\subseteq[n]$ with $|I|=|J|=k$ . If there exist distinct indices $r\neq r^{\prime}\in[n]$ such that $I\leq_{r}J$ and $I\leq_{r^{\prime}}J$ , then $\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}=\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r^{\prime}}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,r}=\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,r^{\prime}}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,r}=\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}\cap\{\Delta_{I}\Delta_{J}\neq 0\}$ , it suffices to prove the closed case. By Proposition 4.6, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r} \displaystyle=\{V\in\gr_{k,n}:\Delta_{K}(V)=0\text{ for all }K\notin[I,J]_{r}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\{V\in\gr_{k,n}:\Delta_{K}(V)=0\text{ for all }K\notin[I,J]_{r^{\prime}}\}. $$

Since Lemma 3.10 implies $[I,J]_{r}=[I,J]_{r^{\prime}}$ , we have $\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r}=\mathcal{R}_{I,J,r^{\prime}}$ . ∎

Our main result now follows from Theorem 4.7 and Lemma 4.9.

#### Corollary 4.10.

The varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ are both independent of $\mathbf{a}$ as long as $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ .

As a consequence of Corollary 4.10, we omit the sequence $\mathbf{a}$ and denote the the (open) tilted Richardson varieties simply by $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ . In particular, when $u\leq v$ in Bruhat order, these varieties recover the classical Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=\mathcal{R}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\mathcal{R}_{u,v}$ .

### 4.3. Definition via Plücker Coordinates

In this section, we give yet another characterization of tilted Richardson varieties using the vanishing of certain multi-Plücker coordinates (Theorem 4.12). We begin with the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.11.

Let $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}$ and $I\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ , if $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ , then there exists a permutation $w\in S_{n}$ such that $w[k]=I$ and $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ .

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume $I=[k]$ . We prove the contrapositive statement. Suppose $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for every permutation $w$ with $w[k]=[k]$ . Equivalently, $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for all $w$ where $w\ngeq s_{k}$ in the Bruhat order. It follows from Lemma 2.5 that $F_{\bullet}\in\Omega_{s_{k}}$ . Hence $\Delta_{[k]}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , which is a contradiction. ∎

We now establish our third characterization of tilted Richardson varieties.

#### Theorem 4.12.

For permutations $u,v\in S_{n}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\{F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}:\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0\text{ for all }w\notin[u,v]\}. $$

The corresponding open cell is given by $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap\{\Delta_{u}\Delta_{v}\neq 0\}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{a}$ be a sequence such that $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . Suppose $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ and $w\notin[u,v]$ . By Theorem 3.13, there exists some $k\in[n]$ such that $w[k]\notin[u[k],v[k]]_{a_{k}}$ . Since $F_{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}$ by Theorem 4.7, it follows from Proposition 4.6 that $\Delta_{w[k]}(F_{k})=0$ . Consequently, we obtain $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , which proves the inclusion $\subseteq$ .

Conversely, suppose $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for all $w\notin[u,v]$ . If $F_{\bullet}\notin\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ , by Proposition 4.6, there exists some $k\in[n]$ and $I\in{\binom{[n]}{k}}$ such that $\Delta_{I}(F_{k})\neq 0$ but $I\notin[u[k],v[k]]_{a_{k}}$ . By Lemma 4.11, we find a permutation $w$ such that $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ and $w[k]=I$ , hence $w\notin[u,v]$ . This contradicts our assumption.

Finally, for the open variety $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ , note that $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}=\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}\cap\{\Delta_{u[k]}\Delta_{v[k]}\neq 0\}$ . Therefore, by Theorem 4.7, $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap\{\Delta_{u}\Delta_{v}=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\Delta_{u[k]}\Delta_{v[k]}\neq 0\}$ as desired. ∎

#### Remark 4.13.

One may wonder whether every tilted Richardson variety is trivially isomorphic to some classical Richardson variety. Specifically, given $u,v\in S_{n}$ , does there always exist $w\in S_{n}$ such that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=w\mathcal{R}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}$ for some classical Richardson variety $\mathcal{R}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}$ ? Computational checks on the level of $T$ -fixed points show that this is not always true. For example, when $u=512346$ and $v=246513$ , the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ is not equal to $w\cdot[u^{\prime},v^{\prime}]$ for any classical Bruhat interval $[u^{\prime},v^{\prime}]$ and $w\in S_{n}$ . Thus, tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ are a genuinely new class of varieties.

### 4.4. Definition via Tilted Schubert Cells

In this section, we introduce tilted Schubert cells $X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ and opposite tilted Schubert cells $\Omega_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ for a permutation $w\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , and show that their intersections $X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ define the open tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ whenever $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ (Theorem 4.21). We start with some definitions.

#### Definition 4.14.

Given $w\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , the tilted Rothe diagram is defined as the following subset of an $n\times n$ grid:

$$ D_{\mathbf{a}}(w):=\{(w_{i},k)\in[n]^{2}:i>k,\ w_{i}<_{a_{k}}w_{k}\}. $$

Similarly, the opposite tilted Rothe diagram is defined as:

$$ D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)=\{(w_{i},k)\in[n]^{2}:i>k,\ w_{i}>_{a_{k}}w_{k}\}. $$

It is obvious that the numbers of cells in these diagrams are directly related to the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted length $\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ as defined in Definition 3.17. Specifically, $|D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)|=\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ and $|D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)|=\binom{n}{2}-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ . We now illustrate Definition 4.14 with a concrete example below.

#### Example 4.15.

Consider $w=4321$ and $\mathbf{a}=(4,4,2,2)$ . We draw the diagrams in Figure 10 as follows. Place a $\bullet$ at position $(w_{k},k)$ for each $k\in[4]$ . Draw a red horizontal line at each column $k$ at the cutoff for $\leq_{a_{k}}$ . For $D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ , draw rays to the right and down from each $\bullet$ until they hit the red line or the right boundary. Similarly, for $D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)$ , draw rays to the right and up. The green boxes remaining represent the tilted Rothe daigrams $D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ and $D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)$ , respectively.

*(b) $D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)=\{(1,1),(2,1),(3,1),(1,3)\}$*

*Figure 10. Tilted Rothe diagrams for $w=4321$ and $\mathbf{a}=(4,4,2,2)$*

One may notice similarities between Figure 10(a) and the classical Rothe diagram of a permutation introduced in [42]. Indeed, when $\mathbf{a}=(1,\dots,1)$ , the tilted Rothe diagram $D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ recovers the classical Rothe diagram of the permutation $w^{-1}$ .

We now define the tilted analogues of Schubert and opposite Schubert cells.

#### Definition 4.16.

Given $w\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , define the tilted Schubert cell as

$$ X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}:=\{F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}:\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0\text{ and }\Delta_{w[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0\text{ for all }(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)\}. $$

Similarly, define the opposite tilted Schubert cell as

$$ \Omega^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}:=\{F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}:\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0\text{ and }\Delta_{w[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0\text{ for all }(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)\}. $$

The next proposition provides an explicit matrix representative for flags in these tilted Schubert cells, which we call the canonical representative or the canonical matrix.

#### Proposition 4.17.

A flag $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}$ (resp. $\Omega^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}$ ) if and only if $F_{\bullet}$ is represented by a matrix $M_{F}=(m_{i,k})_{i,k\in[n]}$ such that

$$ m_{i,k}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{ if }i=w_{k},\\
\ast,&\text{ if }(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)\text{ (resp. $D_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{op}}(w)$)},\\
0,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Here $\ast$ represents an arbitrary number in $\mathbb{C}$ . Consequently, we have

$$ X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cong\mathbb{C}^{\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(w)}\quad\text{and}\quad\Omega_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cong\mathbb{C}^{\binom{n}{2}-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(w)}. $$

#### Proof.

We prove the result for the case $X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ ; the case for $\Omega_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ is similar. By performing column reduction, the condition $\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ implies that $F_{\bullet}$ can be represented by a unique matrix $M_{F}=(m_{i,k})_{i,k\in[n]}$ with $1$ ’s at positions $(w_{k},k)$ for all $k\in[n]$ and $0$ ’s to the right of these $1$ ’s. The conditions on the remaining entries follow from the fact that $m_{i,k}=0\iff\Delta_{w[k-1]\cup\{i\}}=0$ for each $(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ . ∎

#### Example 4.18.

We demonstrate Proposition 4.17 with $w=4321$ and $\mathbf{a}=(4,4,2,2)$ using diagrams in Figure 11. We suggest the readers to compare them with the tilted Rothe diagrams from Figure 10.

*(a) $X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$*

*(b) $\Omega_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$*

*Figure 11. Canonical representatives of tilted Schubert cells for $w=4321$ and $\mathbf{a}=(4,4,2,2)$*

#### Remark 4.19.

When $\mathbf{a}=(1,1,\dots,1)$ , we recover the classical Schubert cells $X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}=X_{w}^{\circ}$ and $\Omega_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}=\Omega_{w}^{\circ}$ . In this case, the canonical matrices in Proposition 4.17 coincide with the canonical representatives of Schubert cells in Section 2.2.3.

As a consequence of Proposition 4.17, we obtain a tilted Bruhat decomposition of the flag variety into tilted Schubert cells, in analogy with the classical Bruhat decomposition:

#### Lemma 4.20.

Let $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ . The tilted Schubert cells define the following decomposition of the flag variety:

$$ \fl_{n}=\bigsqcup_{w\in S_{n}}X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}=\bigsqcup_{w\in S_{n}}\Omega^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}. $$

#### Proof.

For any point $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}$ , there is a unique way to reduce $F_{\bullet}$ to its canonical representative as described in Proposition 4.17, using column operations. From this representative, one can uniquely determine a permutation $w$ such that $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}$ . The argument for the decomposition using $\Omega^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}$ is similar. ∎

Finally, we state the main result of this section, which establishes the relationship between tilted Richardson varieties and the intersections of tilted Schubert and opposite tilted Schubert cells.

#### Theorem 4.21.

For permutations $u,v\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ ,

- (1) if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , then $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\subseteq X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ ;

- (2) if $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , then $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

#### Proof.

In fact, we prove the following stronger version of the theorem: for any $u,v\in S_{n}$ and $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , we have (1) $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}\subseteq X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ ; (2) if $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , then $\mathcal{T}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}=X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ . The original theorem then follows by restricting to the case $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ .

To prove (1), we focus on proving $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}\subseteq\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ , as the proof for $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}\subseteq X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ is similar. Our goal is to show that any $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}$ satisfies the Plücker conditions in Definition 4.16. By Theorem 4.12, we already have $\Delta_{u}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ . It remains to verify that $\Delta_{u[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for all $(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ . This follows from the fact that $i<_{a_{k}}u_{k}$ implies $u[k-1]\cup\{i\}<_{a_{k}}u[k]$ . Since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})$ , by Proposition 4.6 we have $\Delta_{u[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , as required.

To prove (2), it suffices to show the $\supseteq$ direction. Equivalently, we must verify that

$$ X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}\cap\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}\subseteq\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})\text{ for all }k\in[n-1]. $$

We proceed by induction on $k$ . For the base case $k=1$ , we must show that every $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}\cap\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ satisfies $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u_{1},v_{1},a_{1}})$ . Since $F_{\bullet}\in\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ implies $\Delta_{u_{1}}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ , and $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}$ implies $\Delta_{v_{1}}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ , it remains to verify that $\Delta_{i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for all $i\in[a_{1},u_{1})_{c}\cup(v_{1},a_{1}-1]_{c}$ . The case $i\in[a_{1},u_{1})_{c}$ follows directly from the Plücker conditions on $\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ , while the case $i\in(v_{1},a_{1}-1]_{c}$ follows from those on $X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}$ .

For the induction step, we need to show the following implication:

$$ F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k-1}})\cap X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}\cap\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}\implies F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}). $$

Since $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , it follows from Lemma 4.9 that $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k-1}}=\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k}}$ . Our goal is to show that $F_{\bullet}$ satisfies the Plücker conditions given in Proposition 4.6: that is, if $I\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k]$ or $I\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ , then $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})=0$ . We prove the case $I\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k]$ , as the case $I\nleq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ follows by a similar argument.

To show that $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , we consider the incidence Plücker relation (2.1) associated with $u[k-1]$ and $I$ :

$$ \Delta_{u[k-1]}\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{i\in I\setminus u[k-1]}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{u[k-1]+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

Since $\Delta_{u[k-1]}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ , it suffices to show that each term on the right-hand side vanishes. There are two cases for $i\in I\setminus u[k-1]$ :

- (1) If $i\geq_{a_{k}}u_{k}$ : then the assumption $I\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k]$ implies $I\setminus\{i\}\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k-1]$ . Therefore, $\Delta_{I-i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k}})$ ;

- (2) If $i<_{a_{k}}u_{k}$ : then $(i,k)\in D_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ . Therefore, $\Delta_{u[k-1]+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ .

In either case, each summand on the right-hand side vanishes, and we conclude that $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , as desired. ∎

#### Remark 4.22.

In the classical setting, Schubert cells $X_{w}^{\circ}$ and $\Omega_{w}^{\circ}$ along with their closures, Schubert varieties $X_{w}$ and $\Omega_{w}$ , have many nice geometric properties. Motivated by this, we define tilted Schubert varieties $\overline{X_{v}^{\circ}}$ and $\overline{\Omega_{u}^{\circ}}$ as the closures of the corresponding tilted Schubert cells in the flag variety. However, many aspects of these tilted Schubert cells and varieties remain mysterious, as many properties in the classical setting fail or remain unknown in the tilted setting. We outline several key differences:

- • In the classical case, $\mathcal{R}_{u,v}=X_{v}\cap\Omega_{u}$ . However, in the tilted case, we do not always have $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\overline{X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}}\cap\overline{\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}}$ . For example, when $u=14325$ , $v=15342$ , $\mathbf{a}=(3,3,1,1,1)$ , there exists $w=15243$ , with $e_{w}\in\overline{X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}}\cap\overline{\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}}$ but $e_{w}\notin\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ .

- • In the classical setting, every Schubert variety $X_{w}$ or $\Omega_{w}$ can be realized as a Richardson variety. However, there exist tilted Schubert varieties that do not coincide with any tilted Richardson varieties. For example, when $w=2314$ and $\mathbf{a}=(3,3,1,1)$ , $\overline{X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}}$ does not equal any tilted Richardson variety. This is evident by examining the set of $T$ -fixed points in $\overline{X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}}$ , which does not equal any tilted Bruhat interval.

- • The inclusion relations of classical Schubert varieties respect the Bruhat order, satisfying $X_{u}\subseteq X_{v}$ if and only if $u\leq v$ . However, it is not true in general that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ implies $\overline{X^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}}\subseteq\overline{X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}}$ . For example, when $u=13245$ , $v=23145$ , and $\mathbf{a}=(3,3,1,1,1)$ , we find that for $w=35241$ , $e_{w}\in\overline{X^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}}$ but $e_{w}\notin\overline{X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}}$ .

- • Given a sequence $\mathbf{a}$ , the tilted Bruhat decomposition $\fl_{n}=\bigsqcup_{w\in S_{n}}X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}$ is not necessarily a stratification. For example, when $w=3124$ and $\mathbf{a}=(3,3,1,1)$ , the tilted Schubert variety $\overline{X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}}$ is not a union of tilted Schubert cells. Specifically, we have $X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cong\mathbb{C}$ and $\overline{X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}=X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cup\{e_{v}\}$ for $v=3421$ , but $\{e_{v}\}$ is not a tilted Schubert cell for $\mathbf{a}$ since $\{e_{v}\}\subsetneq X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

#### Conjecture 4.23.

If $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , then $X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ intersect transversely.

Conjecture 4.23 would imply that the tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ is smooth.

#### Problem 4.24.

Describe all $T$ -fixed points in the tilted Schubert variety $\overline{X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}}$ explicitly.

We know $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ implies $e_{u}\in\overline{X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}}}$ , but it is not enough to determine all $T$ -fixed points.

## 5. Geometric Properties of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we establish some fundamental geometric properties of the tilted Richardson varieties, analogous to those of the Richardson varieties. In particular, we show that:

- (1) There is a stratification $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]}\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ indexed by subintervals of the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ (Section 5.1);

- (2) The dimensions of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ are given by the length of the shortest path from $u$ to $v$ in the quantum Bruhat graph (Section 5.2);

- (3) The closure relation $\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ holds (Section 5.3).

Our proofs differ substantially from Richardson’s original proof of these results for classical Richardson varieties in [48], which heavily relies on the fact that the Richardson variety $\mathcal{R}_{u,v}$ arises as the transverse intersection of two opposite Schubert varieties $X_{v}\cap\Omega_{u}$ , or equivalently, as the intersection of two opposite Borel orbits $BvB\cap B_{-}uB$ in the flag variety. In contrast, tilted Richardson varieties do not inherit this orbit intersection structure, requiring us to develop new methods to establish their geometric properties.

### 5.1. A Stratification of Tilted Richardson Varieties

#### Theorem 5.1.

There is a stratification $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]}\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ indexed by subintervals $[x,y]$ of the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ .

#### Proof.

It follows directly from Definition 4.1 that the strata $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{x,y}$ on the right-hand side are disjoint and each stratum $\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ is contained in $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ for all subintervals $[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]$ . It remains to show that for any $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ , there exists $[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]$ such that $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ .

We fix a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 3.12. For each $k\in[n]$ , since $F_{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}$ , and since $\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}$ admits a stratification $\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}=\bigsqcup_{I,J}\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I,J,a_{k}}$ , the subspace $F_{k}$ must lie in one of these strata, say $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I_{k},J_{k},a_{k}}$ for some subsets $I_{k},J_{k}\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ satisfying $u[k]\leq_{a_{k}}I_{k}\leq_{a_{k}}J_{k}\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ .

We now show that $I_{k-1}\subseteq I_{k}$ for every $k\in[n]$ . Consider the incidence Plücker relation (2.1) associated with $I_{k-1}$ and $I_{k}$ :

$$ \Delta_{I_{k-1}}\Delta_{I_{k}}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{i\in I_{k}\setminus I_{k-1}}\Delta_{I_{k}-i}\Delta_{I_{k-1}+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

Since the left-hand side is nonzero, at least one term $\Delta_{I_{k}-i}\Delta_{I_{k-1}+i}(F_{\bullet})$ on the right-hand side must also be nonzero for some $i\in I_{k}\setminus I_{k-1}$ . Because $F_{k}\in\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I_{k},J_{k},a_{k}}$ , Proposition 4.6 and $\Delta_{I_{k-1}+i}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ implies that $I_{k-1}\cup\{i\}\geq_{a_{k}}I_{k}$ . On the other hand, using the condition $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and Lemma 4.9, we have $F_{k-1}\in\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I_{k},J_{k},a_{k-1}}=\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{I_{k-1},J_{k-1},a_{k}}$ , implying $I_{k}\setminus\{i\}\geq_{a_{k}}I_{k-1}$ , or equivalently $I_{k}\geq_{a_{k}}I_{k-1}\cup\{i\}$ . These inequalities can only hold if $I_{k}=I_{k-1}\cup\{i\}$ , confirming $I_{k-1}\subseteq I_{k}$ . Similarly, we obtain $J_{k-1}\subseteq J_{k}$ for every $k\in[n]$ .

Finally, we define permutations $x,y\in S_{n}$ by setting $x_{k}=I_{k}\setminus I_{k-1}$ and $y_{k}=J_{k}\setminus J_{k-1}$ for all $k\in[n]$ . It follows from Theorem 4.7 that $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ . Since $u[k]\leq_{a_{k}}I_{k}\leq_{a_{k}}J_{k}\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ for all $k\in[n]$ , we conclude that $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}x\leq_{\mathbf{a}}y\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , and thus $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{x,y}$ for some subinterval $[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]$ . ∎

### 5.2. Dimensions of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we show that the dimension of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is given by $\ell(u,v)$ , the length of the shortest path from $u$ to $v$ in the quantum Bruhat graph (Theorem 5.4). The key observation is that since $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is the intersection $X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ by Theorem 4.21, its codimension is at most the sum of the codimensions of the tilted Schubert cells $X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ and $\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

For any permutation $x\in S_{n}$ , the affine chart $x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ is the permuted opposite Schubert cell, consisting of flags satisfying $\Delta_{x}\neq 0$ . These flags can also be represented by matrices with $1$ ’s at positions $(x_{k},k)$ for all $k\in[n]$ and $0$ ’s to the right of $1$ ’s.

#### Example 5.2.

Let $x=3142$ . The affine chart $x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ can be identified as the following affine space, where each $*$ represents an arbitrary number in $\mathbb{C}$ :

The following lemma describes the relationship between tilted Richardson varieties, open tilted Richardson varieties, and affine charts. In particular, it shows that the open tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ are quasi-affine varieties.

#### Lemma 5.3.

For any permutations $u,v,x\in S_{n}$ ,

- (1) if $x\notin[u,v]$ , then $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=\emptyset$ ,

- (2) $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap v\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ .

#### Proof.

This result follows directly from Theorem 4.12. ∎

We are now ready to state the dimension formula.

#### Theorem 5.4.

The open tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ is equidimensional of dimension $\ell(u,v)$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $\ell(u,v)$ . In the base case $\ell(u,v)=0$ , or $u=v$ , the statement is immediate since $\mathcal{T}_{u,u}^{\circ}=\{e_{u}\}$ is a single point.

Fix a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 3.12. Since $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ by Theorem 4.21, $\codim(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v})$ is at most the sum of $\codim(X_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ})$ and $\codim(\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ})$ . These values are given by $\binom{n}{2}-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ and $\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ , respectively. Thus,

$$ \codim(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ})\leq\codim(X^{\circ}_{v,\mathbf{a}})+\codim(\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\binom{n}{2}-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)+\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(u). $$

By Corollary 3.19, $\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(u)=\ell(u,v)$ , and thus every irreducible component of $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ has dimension at least $\ell(u,v)$ .

It remains to show $\dim(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v})\leq\ell(u,v)$ . Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists an irreducible component $Z\subseteq\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ with $\dim(Z)\geq\ell(u,v)+1$ . Let $\overline{Z}$ be the closure of $Z$ in $\fl_{n}$ and define its boundary as $\partial Z:=\overline{Z}\setminus Z$ . By Lemma 5.3, $Z=\overline{Z}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap v\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ . Therefore,

$$ \partial Z=\overline{Z}\cap(\fl_{n}\setminus(u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap v\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}))=\overline{Z}\cap\{\Delta_{u}\Delta_{v}=0\}. $$

We consider two cases:

- (1) If $\partial Z\neq\emptyset$ , then since $\partial Z$ is the intersection of $\overline{Z}$ with a union of hypersurfaces $\{\Delta_{u}\Delta_{v}=0\}$ , we have $\dim(\partial Z)\geq\dim(\overline{Z})-1\geq\ell(u,v)$ . However, from Theorem 5.1, $\partial Z\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\setminus\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{[x,y]\subsetneq[u,v]}\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{x,y}$ . By the induction hypothesis, each $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{x,y}$ has dimension at most $\ell(x,y)\leq\ell(u,v)-1$ , hence $\dim(\partial Z)\leq\ell(u,v)-1$ , a contradiction.

- (2) If $\partial Z=\emptyset$ , then $Z=\overline{Z}$ is a projective variety. However, $Z\subseteq u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap v\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ is quasi-affine. This is only possible if $Z$ is a point, contradicting $\dim(Z)\geq\ell(u,v)+1\geq 1$ .

Since both cases lead to a contradiction, we conclude that $\dim(Z)=\ell(u,v)$ , and thus every irreducible component of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ has dimension $\ell(u,v)$ . ∎

### 5.3. Closure Relations of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we prove the closure relation $\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ (Theorem 5.11). While one direction $\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is immediate from the definition, the other direction requires a more delicate analysis of the geometry of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ on different affine charts.

We now outline the strategy of the proof. The argument proceeds by induction on $\ell(u,v)$ . By Theorem 5.1, it is enough to show that $\mathcal{T}_{u,x}^{\circ}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}$ for all $x\in[u,v]$ such that $\ell(u,x)=\ell(u,v)-1$ , and dually, $\mathcal{T}_{y,v}^{\circ}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}$ for all $y\in[u,v]$ such that $\ell(y,v)=\ell(u,v)-1$ . We focus on the first case.

To prove this, we introduce a new subvariety of $\fl_{n}$ , called the skew tilted Schubert cell $X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ (Definition 5.6). It is closely related to the tilted Schubert cell from Definition 4.16, and is isomorphic to an affine space $\mathbb{C}^{\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)}$ . A key step in the argument is to show that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ (Proposition 5.10). This identity allows us to lower-bound the dimension of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ , which ultimately leads the desired closure relation via a straightforward geometric argument.

We begin with a lemma that focuses on the intersection $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ , which effectively “isolates” the two relevant strata $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,x}^{\circ}$ .

#### Lemma 5.5.

For any $u,v,x\in S_{n}$ such that $x\in[u,v]$ and $\ell(u,x)=\ell(u,v)-1$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=\mathcal{T}_{u,x}^{\circ}\sqcup(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}). $$

#### Proof.

By Theorem 5.1, there is a decomposition $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]}\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ . According to Lemma 5.3, the only strata that intersect both $u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ and $x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ are $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,x}$ and $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ , which implies the claim. ∎

We now define the skew tilted Schubert cells.

#### Definition 5.6.

Fix $x,v\in S_{n}$ and a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $x\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\lesssim$\cr\raise 1.93747pt\hbox{$\cdot\mkern 1.0mu$}\cr}}}_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $x=vt_{pq}$ for $p<q$ . Define the following subsets of an $n\times n$ grid (the second is the tilted Rothe diagram from Definition 4.14):

$$ \displaystyle D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v) \displaystyle:=\{(x_{i},k)\in[n]^{2}:i>k,\ x_{i}<_{a_{k}}v_{k}\}, \displaystyle D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x) \displaystyle:=\{(x_{i},k)\in[n]^{2}:i>k,\ x_{i}<_{a_{k}}x_{k}\}. $$

The skew tilted Schubert cell $X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ is defined as the set of flags $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}$ satisfying the following Plücker conditions:

- (1) $\Delta_{x}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ ;

- (2) $\Delta_{x[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0$ for all $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\cap D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ ;

- (3) For all $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\setminus D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ (necessarily with $k=q$ ), we require:

$$ \Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{x[q]}(F_{\bullet})=\Delta_{x[q-1]+i}\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}(F_{\bullet}). $$

We claim that $|D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)|=\binom{n}{2}-\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ and that the skew tilted Schubert cell satisfies $X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cong\mathbb{C}^{\ell_{\mathbf{a}}(v)}$ . Instead of giving a formal proof for these claims, they will become clear once we present the following example for Definition 5.6.

We are ready to prove Proposition 5.10, which relies on the following two lemmas.

#### Lemma 5.8.

Let $I\in\binom{[n]}{a},J\in\binom{[n]}{b}$ with $1\leq b<a<n$ . Suppose there exists an integer $k\in(b,a)$ and subsets $K_{1},K_{2}\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ such that for some $r,r^{\prime}\in[n]$ , we have $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{R}_{K_{1},K_{2},r}=\mathcal{R}_{K_{1},K_{2},r^{\prime}}$ . Then the following identity holds:

$$ \sum_{i\in I\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

#### Proof.

Fix any $K\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ such that $\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ . Multiply the desired expression by $\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})$ , and expand $\Delta_{J+i}\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})$ using (2.3), the left hand side becomes

$$ \sum_{i\in I\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+i}\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}\\
j\in K\end{subarray}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+j}\Delta_{K-j+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

By Proposition 4.6, $\Delta_{K-j+i}(F_{\bullet})$ is nonzero only if $K\setminus\{j\}\cup\{i\}\in[K_{1},K_{2}]_{r}=[K_{1},K_{2}]_{r^{\prime}}$ , which by Lemma 3.10 implies $i,j\in[r,r^{\prime})_{c}$ . So the sum above can be rewritten as

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}\\
j\in K\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+j}\Delta_{K-j+i}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\\
j\in K\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+j}\Delta_{K-j+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

For each fixed $j\in K\cap[r,r^{\prime})_{c}$ , $\sum_{i\in I}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{K-j+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ by (2.2), completing the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 5.9.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ and $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . For any subsets $I\in\binom{[n]}{q}$ , $J\in\binom{[n]}{p-1}$ with $1\leq p<q<n$ , suppose a flag $F_{\bullet}$ satisfies $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})$ for every $p\leq k<q$ . Then the following identity holds:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\cap[a_{p},a_{q})_{c}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

#### Proof.

For each integer $k$ with $p\leq k<q$ , Lemma 5.8 gives the relation:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\cap[a_{k},a_{k+1})_{c}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

Summing these equations over $k=p,\dots,q-1$ , and subtracting the full-sum relation $\sum_{i\in I}\Delta_{I-i}\Delta_{J+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ (as given by (2.2)) the appropriate number of times, we obtain the desired result. ∎

We are now ready to prove the key intersection result of this section.

#### Proposition 5.10.

Let $u,v,x\in S_{n}$ and $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , $x\in[u,v]$ and $\ell(u,x)=\ell(u,v)-1$ . Then, we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}. $$

As a consequence, the intersection $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ is equidimensional of dimension $\ell(u,v)$ .

#### Proof.

Throughout this proof, we assume that $x=vt_{pq}$ for some integers $p<q$ . We begin by proving the containment $\subseteq$ . Since the left-hand side lies in $\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ by Theorem 4.21, it suffices to show that

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\subseteq X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}. $$

That is, we need to verify that any flag $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ satisfies the Plücker conditions listed in Definition 5.6. Since $F_{\bullet}\in x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ , we already have $\Delta_{x}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ . It remains to verify the two additional types of Plücker conditions.

We first verify condition (2) of Definition 5.6. For all $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\cap D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , we claim that $x[k-1]\cup\{i\}\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ . This will imply $\Delta_{x[k-1]\cup\{i\}}(F_{\bullet})=0$ by Proposition 4.6, since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})$ . The claim follows by case analysis:

- (1) If $k<p$ or $k>q$ : then $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}(x,v)$ implies $i>_{a_{k}}v_{k}$ , so $x[k-1]\cup\{i\}>_{a_{k}}v[k]$ ;

- (2) If $k=q$ : then $(i,q)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}(x)$ implies $i>_{a_{q}}x_{q}$ , so $x[k-1]\cup\{i\}>_{a_{k}}v[k]$ ;

- (3) If $p<k<q$ : suppose for contradiction that $x[k-1]\cup\{i\}\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ . Then we must have $\{i,v_{q}\}\leq_{a_{k}}\{v_{k},v_{p}\}$ . But $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}(x,v)$ implies $i>_{a_{k}}v_{k}$ , so we must have $v_{q}<_{a_{k}}v_{k}<_{a_{k}}i\leq_{a_{k}}v_{p}$ , which contradicts the condition $x=vt_{pq}\lessdot_{\mathbf{a}}v$ by Proposition 3.15.

We now verify condition (3) of Definition 5.6. For all $(i,q)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\setminus D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , we apply the incidence Plücker relation from (2.3):

$$ \Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{x[q]}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{k\in[p,q]}\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{k}}\Delta_{x[q]-x_{k}+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

Moving the $k=q$ term to the left-hand side, we obtain:

$$ \Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{x[q]}(F_{\bullet})-\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}\Delta_{x[q-1]+i}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{k\in[p,q)}\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{k}}\Delta_{x[q]-x_{k}+i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

Since the left-hand side matches condition (3), it remains to show that the right-hand side vanishes. We analyze the terms in the right-hand side through the following cases:

- (1) If $k=p$ : then $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}(x,v)$ implies $i>_{a_{q}}v_{q}$ , so $x[q]\setminus\{x_{p}\}\cup\{i\}>_{a_{q}}v[q]$ . Hence, $\Delta_{x[q]-x_{p}+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ by Proposition 4.6, since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{q}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[q],v[q],a_{q}})$ ;

- (2) If $p<k<q$ and $x_{k}>_{a_{p}}x_{q}$ : then $x[p-1]\cup\{x_{k}\}>_{a_{p}}v[p]$ , so $\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{k}}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{p}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[p],v[p],a_{p}})$ ;

- (3) If $p<k<q$ and $i>_{a_{q}}x_{k}$ : then $x[q]\setminus\{x_{k}\}\cup\{i\}>_{a_{q}}v[q]$ , so $\Delta_{x[q]-x_{k}+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{q}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[q],v[q],a_{q}})$ ;

- (4) In the remaining case where $p<k<q$ and none of the above apply, the following conditions must hold: (a) $x_{k}\leq_{a_{p}}x_{q}$ , and by Proposition 3.15, this can be strengthened to $x_{k}<_{a_{p}}x_{p}<_{a_{p}}x_{q}$ ; (b) $i\leq_{a_{q}}x_{k}$ ; (c) Additionally, since $(i,q)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\setminus D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , we have $x_{p}<_{a_{q}}i<_{a_{q}}x_{q}$ . Placing these six integers on a circle in an increasing order (clockwise), we observe the following cyclic configuration (up to rotation):

$$ a_{p}\leq x_{k}<a_{q}\leq x_{p}<i<x_{q}<a_{p}. $$

In this setting, the right-hand side simplifies to

$$ \sum_{x_{k}\in[a_{p},a_{q})_{c}}\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{k}}\Delta_{x[q]-x_{k}+i}(F_{\bullet}), $$

which vanishes by Lemma 5.9.

We now prove the $\supseteq$ direction. Since, by definition, the right-hand side $X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ is contained in both $x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ and $u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}$ , it suffices to show that $X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ , or equivalently,

$$ X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\subseteq\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}})\text{ for all }k\in[n]. $$

We proceed by induction on $k$ . The overall structure, including the base case, is the same as in the proof of Theorem 4.21. For the induction step, we must show the implication:

$$ F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k-1}})\cap X^{\circ}_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}\cap\Omega^{\circ}_{u,\mathbf{a}}\implies F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k],v[k],a_{k}}). $$

Since $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , it follows from Lemma 4.9 that $\mathcal{R}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k-1}}=\mathcal{R}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k}}$ . Our goal is to show that $F_{\bullet}$ satisfies the Plücker conditions in Proposition 4.6: that is, if $K\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k]$ or $K\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ , then $\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})=0$ . The case $K\not\geq_{a_{k}}u[k]$ is handled exactly as in the proof of Theorem 4.21, so we focus on the case $K\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ .

To show that $\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , we consider the incidence Plücker relation (2.1) associated with $x[k-1]$ and $K$ :

$$ \Delta_{x[k-1]}\Delta_{K}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{i\in K\setminus x[k-1]}\Delta_{x[k-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

Since $\Delta_{x[k-1]}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ , it suffices to show that right-hand side vanishes. We analyze each term on the right-hand side by considering the following three cases for $i\in K\setminus x[k-1]$ :

- (1) If $i\leq_{a_{k}}v_{k}$ : then the assumption $K\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ implies $K\setminus\{i\}\not\leq_{a_{k}}v[k-1]$ . Therefore, $\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[k-1],v[k-1],a_{k}})$ ;

- (2) If $i>_{a_{k}}v_{k}$ and $i>_{a_{k}}x_{k}$ : then $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\cap D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , Therefore, $\Delta_{x[k-1]+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}$ .

- (3) If $i>_{a_{k}}v_{k}$ but $i\leq_{a_{k}}x_{k}$ : this scenario occurs only when $k=q$ , $i\in[x_{p},x_{q})_{c}$ , and $(i,k)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}(x,v)\setminus D^{\mathrm{op}}(x)$ . In this case, we must show that the sum

$$ \sum_{i\in K\cap(x_{p},x_{q}]_{c}}\Delta_{x[q-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet}) $$

vanishes. To prove this, we wish to multiply both sides by $\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}(F_{\bullet})$ and apply condition (3) from Definition 5.6. Although it is not guaranteed that $\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}(F_{\bullet})$ is nonzero, in the degenerate case where it vanishes (e.g., when $a=0$ in Figure 13), the Plücker conditions in Definition 5.6 reduce precisely to those defining $X_{x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ in Definition 4.16. This implies that $F_{\bullet}\in X_{x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ in such case. Therefore, by Theorem 4.21, we conclude that

$$ F_{\bullet}\in X_{x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}=\mathcal{T}_{u,x}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}. $$

Hence, we may safely assume that $\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ . Multiplying both sides by this nonzero Plücker coordinate and applying condition (3) from Definition 5.6, we obtain:

$$ \sum_{i\in K\cap(x_{p},x_{q}]_{c}}\Delta_{x[p-1]+x_{q}}\Delta_{x[q-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=\sum_{i\in K\cap(x_{p},x_{q}]_{c}}\Delta_{x[q]}\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet}). $$

To prove the vanishing of the right-hand side, we divide the sum into three parts and show that each of them vanishes: (a) For $i\in K\cap(x_{q},a_{p})_{c}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i\in K\cap(x_{q},a_{p})_{c}}\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

This is because each term vanishes individually: since $i>_{a_{p}}x_{q}$ , we have $(i,p)\in D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x,v)\cap D^{\mathrm{op}}_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ . Therefore, $\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in X^{\circ}_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}$ . (b) For $i\in K\cap[a_{q},x_{p}]_{c}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i\in K\cap[a_{q},x_{p}]_{c}}\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

This is because each term vanishes individually: since $i\leq_{a_{q}}x_{p}$ , the assumption $K\not\leq_{a_{q}}v[q]$ implies $K\setminus\{i\}\not\leq_{a_{q}}v[q-1]$ . Therefore, $\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , since $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{q-1}^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{u[q-1],v[q-1],a_{q}})$ . (c) For $i\in K\cap[a_{p},a_{q})_{c}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i\in K\cap[a_{p},a_{q})_{c}}\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0. $$

This follows directly from Lemma 5.9 and the induction hypothesis. Combining these three identities and subtracting their sum from the full-sum relation

$$ \sum_{i\in K}\Delta_{x[p-1]+i}\Delta_{K-i}(F_{\bullet})=0 $$

(as given by (2.2)), we conclude that the original right-hand side vanishes.

In either case, we have shown that $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})=0$ , as required. This completes the induction and establishes the intersection claim in the theorem.

Finally, for the dimension statement, since

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=X_{v,x,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\cap\Omega_{u,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ} $$

is cut out by $\binom{n}{2}-\ell(u,v)$ equations, every irreducible component has dimension at least $\ell(u,v)$ . On the other hand, by Theorem 5.4, every irreducible component has dimension at most $\ell(u,v)$ . Hence, the intersection is equidimensional of dimension $\ell(u,v)$ . ∎

Finally, we arrive at the desired closure result.

#### Theorem 5.11.

For all $u,v\in S_{n}$ , we have $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $\ell(u,v)$ . the base case $\ell(u,v)=0$ corresponds to $u=v$ , in which case $\mathcal{T}_{u,u}=\mathcal{T}_{u,u}^{\circ}=\{e_{u}\}$ , so the claim holds.

Now assume $\ell(u,v)>0$ . By Theorem 5.1, it suffices to show that $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,x}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}$ for all $x\in[u,v]$ with $\ell(u,x)=\ell(u,v)-1$ . From Lemma 5.5, we have the decomposition

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}=\mathcal{T}_{u,x}^{\circ}\sqcup(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}). $$

Taking closures on both sides yields

$$ \overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}=\mathcal{T}_{u,x}\cup\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}. $$

Let $Z$ be an irreducible component of the left-hand side. By Proposition 5.10, we know that $\dim(Z)=\ell(u,v)$ . On the other hand, by Theorem 5.4, $\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u,x})=\ell(u,x)=\ell(u,v)-1$ , so $Z$ cannot be contained in $\mathcal{T}_{u,x}$ . Therefore, $Z$ must be contained in $\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}$ . Since this holds for every irreducible components $Z$ , we conclude that

$$ \overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}. $$

Now by applying Lemma 5.5 again, we obtain

$$ \mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,x}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}\cap u\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}\cap x\Omega_{\mathrm{id}}^{\circ}}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

## 6. Tilted Deodhar Decomposition and Its Applications

In this section, we introduce the tilted Deodhar decomposition of tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ , in analogy with the classical Deodhar decomposition of Richardson varieties $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ . This decomposition plays a central role in proving the irreducibility of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and has further applications in the development of a theory of tilted Kazhdan–Lusztig $R$ -polynomials $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)$ and total positivity for tilted Richardson varieties.

### 6.1. Tilted Distinguished Subwords and Regular Tilted Reduced Words

We introduce tilted distinguished subwords (Definition 6.3) and regular tilted reduced words (Definition 6.6), which serve as the combinatorial data labeling each cell in the tilted Deodhar decomposition. For background on tilted reduced words, see Section 3.4. We begin by establishing some notation that will be used consistently throughout the section.

#### Notation 6.1.

Let $\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in[n]^{n}$ be a sequence, and let the set of jumps of $\mathbf{a}$ be denoted by $\Jump_{\mathbf{a}}={\jump_{1}<\jump_{2}<\cdots<\jump_{t}}$ , where $t:=\left|\Jump_{\mathbf{a}}\right|$ .

Let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be a $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v\in S_{n}$ of length $\ell$ . Define the index sets of bar and non-bar factors in $\mathbf{v}$ as

$$ \displaystyle J_{\mathbf{v}}^{\mid} \displaystyle:=\{j\in[\ell]:\text{the $j$-th factor of $\mathbf{v}$ is a bar}\}, \displaystyle J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s} \displaystyle:=\{j\in[\ell]:\text{the $j$-th factor of $\mathbf{v}$ is a non-bar factor $s_{i_{j}}$}\}. $$

Let $\mathbf{u}$ be a subword of $\mathbf{v}$ corresponding to $u\in S_{n}$ . For $0\leq j\leq\ell$ , let $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ and $\mathbf{u}^{(j)}$ denote the subsequences consisting of the first $j$ factors of $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ , respectively. Define $v^{(j)}\in S_{n}$ and $u^{(j)}\in S_{n}$ to be the products of the first $j$ factors of $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ , respectively, with the convention that $v^{(0)}=u^{(0)}=\mathrm{id}$ .

Now define a sequence of sequences $\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{a}^{(\ell-1)},\dots,\mathbf{a}^{(0)}$ in $[n]^{n}$ recursively as follows: start with $\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}:=\mathbf{a}$ , and for each $j=\ell,\dots,1$ , set

$$ \mathbf{a}^{(j-1)}:=\begin{cases}\mathbf{a}^{(j)},&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s},\\
\flatten(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}),&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{\mid}.\end{cases} $$

With this setup, for each $0\leq j\leq\ell$ , the subword $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ is a $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ -tilted reduced word for $v^{(j)}$ , and $\mathbf{u}^{(j)}$ is a subword of $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ corresponding to $u^{(j)}$ .

#### Example 6.2.

Let $n=4$ and $\mathbf{a}=(3,2,2,1)$ . Then the set of jumps is

$$ \Jump_{\mathbf{a}}=\{\jump_{1},\jump_{2}\}=\{1,3\},\quad\text{so }t=2. $$

Let the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v=1423$ be

$$ \mathbf{v}=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid s_{2}s_{1}\mid s_{2}, $$

with total length $\ell=8$ , including $2$ bars. The index sets are:

$$ J_{\mathbf{v}}^{\mid}=\{4,7\},\quad J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s}=\{1,2,3,5,6,8\}. $$

We track the intermediate sequences $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ , permutations $v^{(j)}$ , and sequences $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(0)} \displaystyle=\emptyset \displaystyle v^{(0)} \displaystyle=1234 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(0)} \displaystyle=(1,1,1,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(1)} \displaystyle=s_{1} \displaystyle v^{(1)} \displaystyle=2134 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(1)} \displaystyle=(1,1,1,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(2)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3} \displaystyle v^{(2)} \displaystyle=2143 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(2)} \displaystyle=(1,1,1,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(3)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2} \displaystyle v^{(3)} \displaystyle=2413 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(3)} \displaystyle=(1,1,1,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(4)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid \displaystyle v^{(4)} \displaystyle=2413 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(4)} \displaystyle=(2,2,2,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(5)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid s_{2} \displaystyle v^{(5)} \displaystyle=2143 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(5)} \displaystyle=(2,2,2,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(6)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid s_{2}s_{1} \displaystyle v^{(6)} \displaystyle=1243 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(6)} \displaystyle=(2,2,2,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(7)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid s_{2}s_{1}\mid \displaystyle v^{(7)} \displaystyle=1243 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(7)} \displaystyle=(3,2,2,1) \displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{(8)} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{3}s_{2}\mid s_{2}s_{1}\mid s_{2} \displaystyle v^{(8)} \displaystyle=1423 \displaystyle\mathbf{a}^{(8)} \displaystyle=(3,2,2,1) $$

Notice that for each $j$ , the prefix $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ is an $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ -tilted reduced word for $v^{(j)}$ .

#### Definition 6.3.

Let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v\in S_{n}$ . A subword $\mathbf{u}$ of $\mathbf{v}$ is called a (tilted) distinguished subword if

$$ u^{(j)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(j)}}u^{(j-1)}s_{i_{j}}\text{ for all }j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s}. $$

Equivalently, if right multiplication by $s_{i_{j}}$ decreases $u^{(j-1)}$ in the $\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(j)}}$ order, then we must have $u^{(j)}=u^{(j-1)}s_{i_{j}}$ . We write $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ if $\mathbf{u}$ is a distinguished subword of $\mathbf{v}$ . In this case, define the following index sets:

$$ \displaystyle J^{+}_{\mathbf{u}} \displaystyle:=\{j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s}:u^{(j-1)}<_{\mathbf{a}^{(j)}}u^{(j)}\}, \displaystyle J^{\circ}_{\mathbf{u}} \displaystyle:=\{j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s}:u^{(j-1)}=u^{(j)}\}, \displaystyle J^{-}_{\mathbf{u}} \displaystyle:=\{j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{s}:\;u^{(j-1)}>_{\mathbf{a}^{(j)}}u^{(j)}\}. $$

It follows directly from the definition that if $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ , then for every $0\leq j\leq\ell$ , the prefix $\mathbf{u}^{(j)}$ is a distinguished subword of $\mathbf{v}^{(j)}$ .

#### Example 6.4.

Let $v=246513$ and $\mathbf{a}=(5,5,5,1,1,1)$ . Consider the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ given by

$$ \mathbf{v}=s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid s_{1}s_{2}. $$

There are four distinguished subwords $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ corresponding to $u=512346$ listed below. In each subword, we mark factors $s_{i_{j}}$ with ${\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\widetilde{s_{i_{j}}}}$ when $j\in J^{-}_{\mathbf{u}}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=111111s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid 11 \displaystyle\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=111s_{1}11s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid 1{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\widetilde{s_{2}}} \displaystyle\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=s_{3}1111{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\widetilde{s_{3}}}s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid 11 \displaystyle\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=s_{3}11s_{1}1{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\widetilde{s_{3}}}s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid 1{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\widetilde{s_{2}}} $$

We proceed with the notion of regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted words, which will play an important role in the main theorem of the tilted Deodhar decomposition.

#### Definition 6.5.

A permutation $w\in S_{n}$ is called a Grassmannian permutation if it has at most one descent. It is a bi-Grassmannian permutation if both $w$ and $w^{-1}$ are Grassmannian permutations. For $a,b\in[n]$ , define the bi-Grassmannian permutation $s_{a,b}\in S_{n}$ by

$$ s_{a,b}(i):=\begin{cases}i+a&\text{if }i\leq b,\\
i-b&\text{if }b<i\leq a+b,\\
i&\text{if }i>a+b.\end{cases} $$

Equivalently, in one-line notation,

$$ s_{a,b}=(a+1)\;\cdots\;(a+b)\;1\;\cdots\;a\;(a+b+1)\;\cdots\;n\in S_{n}. $$

#### Definition 6.6.

An $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted word $\mathbf{v}$ for $v\in S_{n}$ is called regular if, for each bar in $\mathbf{v}$ at position $j\in J_{\mathbf{v}}^{\mid}$ , there exists a subsequence of simple transpositions immediately preceding that bar in $\mathbf{v}$ , specifically a subsequence of the form $s_{i_{k+1}}\cdots s_{i_{j-1}}$ (often marked in blue as ${\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{i_{k+1}}\cdots s_{i_{j-1}}}}$ ), which forms a reduced word for the bi-Grassmannian permutation $s_{q-p,p}\in S_{n}$ , where $q:=\jump_{\min}(\mathbf{a}^{(j)})$ and $p:=\#\left\{v[q]\cap[\mathbf{a}^{(j)}_{1},\mathbf{a}^{(j)}_{q})_{c}\right\}$ . In particular, $p$ is the integer appearing in Definition 3.29 for the $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ -flattenable permutation $v^{(j)}$ .

#### Example 6.7.

The $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word from Example 6.4 is regular. The subsequence marked in blue, immediately preceding the bar, has product $s_{2,1}:=312456$ , which satisfies the condition in Definition 6.6:

$$ \mathbf{v}=s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{4}s_{3}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{2}s_{1}}}\mid s_{1}s_{2}. $$

#### Construction 6.8.

We describe an algorithm that constructs a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for any permutation $w\in S_{n}$ . We illustrate the algorithm using the example $\mathbf{a}=(3,3,1,1,1,6)$ and $w=136254$ . The set of jumps of $\mathbf{a}$ in this example is

$$ \Jump_{\mathbf{a}}=\{\jump_{1},\jump_{2},\jump_{3}\}=\{2,5,6\},\quad\text{where }t=3. $$

First, we construct a sequence of permutations:

$$ \mathrm{id}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\tilde{w}^{(t)}\to}w^{(t)}\to\cdots\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\tilde{w}^{(1)}\to}w^{(1)}\to w, $$

where for each $k\in[t]$ , the permutation $w^{(k)}\in S_{n}$ is obtained from $w$ by sorting its first $\jump_{k}$ entries in increasing order with respect to the shifted order $<_{a_{\jump_{k}}}$ , and the permutation ${\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\tilde{w}^{(k)}}\in S_{n}$ is obtained from $w$ by sorting its first $\jump_{k}$ entries in increasing order with respect to the shifted order $<_{a_{\jump_{k}+1}}$ (with the convention that $a_{n+1}=1$ ). In our running example, the resulting sequence is:

$$ 123456\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}123456\to}612345\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}612354\to}123564\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}136254\to}316254\to 136254. $$

Next, for each adjacent pair $w^{\prime}\to w^{\prime\prime}$ in the sequence above, we compute a reduced word for $(w^{\prime})^{-1}w^{\prime\prime}$ , concatenate all these reduced words, and insert a bar after every two reduced word segments to form a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted word for $w$ . In our running example, we obtain:

$$ {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{5}s_{4}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}}}\mid s_{5}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{4}}}\mid s_{2}s_{4}s_{3}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{1}}}\mid s_{1}. $$

All words constructed in this way are regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced words.

Finally, we state the following key lemma.

#### Lemma 6.9.

Any subword of a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word is also regular.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{v}$ be a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word, and let $\mathbf{u}$ be a subword of $\mathbf{v}$ . Since $\mathbf{v}$ is regular, by Definition 6.6, for every bar in $\mathbf{v}$ at position $j\in J^{\mid}_{\mathbf{v}}$ , there exists a subsequence ${\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\overline{s_{i_{k+1}}\cdots s_{i_{j-1}}}}$ immediately preceding the bar that forms a reduced word for the bi-Grassmannian permutation $s_{q-p,p}$ . It remains to show that $\mathbf{u}$ also contains this subsequence immediately before position $j$ , i.e., that $u^{(j)}=u^{(k)}s_{q-p,p}$ . Since $v^{(j)}$ is $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ -flattenable and $v^{(k)}=v^{(j)}s_{q-p,p}$ , we have:

$$ v^{(k)}[q-p]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{q+1},a^{(j)}_{1})_{c},\quad v^{(k)}[q-p+1,q]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{1},a^{(j)}_{q+1})_{c}. $$

Because $\mathbf{v}^{(k)}$ is an $\mathbf{a}^{(k)}$ -tilted reduced word and $\mathbf{u}^{(k)}$ is a subword, Theorem 3.41 implies that $u^{(k)}\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}^{(k)}}v^{(k)}$ . Therefore,

$$ u^{(k)}[q-p]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{q+1},a^{(j)}_{1})_{c},\quad u^{(k)}[q-p+1,q]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{1},a^{(j)}_{q+1})_{c}. $$

On the other hand, since $u^{(j)}$ is $\mathbf{a}^{(j)}$ -flattenable, we have:

$$ u^{(j)}[p]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{1},a^{(j)}_{q+1})_{c},\quad u^{(j)}[p+1,q]\subseteq[a^{(j)}_{q+1},a^{(j)}_{1})_{c}. $$

This implies that $u^{(j)}$ and $u^{(k)}$ have completely swapped the values in the first $q$ positions:

$$ u^{(j)}[p]=u^{(k)}[q-p+1,q],\quad u^{(j)}[p+1,q]=u^{(k)}[q-p]. $$

Hence, the permutation $(u^{(k)})^{-1}u^{(j)}$ sends the values in positions $[q]$ according to $s_{q-p,p}\cdot x$ , where $x\in S_{p}\times S_{q-p}$ is a block permutation that preserves the two segments. Since $s_{q-p,p}\cdot x$ is a subword of $s_{q-p,p}$ , we have $x=\mathrm{id}$ , and $(u^{(k)})^{-1}u^{(j)}=s_{q-p,p}$ , completing the proof. ∎

### 6.2. Tilted Deodhar Decomposition

In this section, we prove the main theorem of the tilted Deodhar decomposition. We begin by introducing the notion of tilted relative position (Definition 6.10), which is analogous to the classical notion of relative position. This leads naturally to the definition of tilted Deodhar cells $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}$ (Proposition 6.12), indexed by an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{v}$ and a distinguished subword $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ . Finally, we state and prove the main theorem of the tilted Deodhar decomposition (Theorem 6.13).

We begin with some definitions. For each $i\in[n-1]$ , let $\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ denote the matrix obtained by replacing the $2\times 2$ block in rows and columns $i$ and $i+1$ of the identity matrix with the given $2\times 2$ matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ . Using this notation, define the following elements of $G$ :

$$ \displaystyle y_{i}(p) \displaystyle=\phi_{i}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
p&1\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle\dot{s}_{i} \displaystyle=\phi_{i}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle x_{i}(m) \displaystyle=\phi_{i}\begin{pmatrix}1&m\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

We now recall the classical notion of relative position (see [43, Section 4.2]), and then introduce the notion of tilted relative position, defined using tilted Schubert cells and the tilted Bruhat decomposition (see Section 4.4).

#### Definition 6.10.

Let $y_{1}=g_{1}B$ , $y_{2}=g_{2}B\in G/B$ . The double coset $y_{1}^{-1}y_{2}=Bg_{1}^{-1}g_{2}B$ is well-defined and equals $BwB$ for some permutation $w\in S_{n}$ by the Bruhat decomposition. We call this permutation the relative position of $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ , and denote it by $y_{1}\xrightarrow{w}y_{2}$ .

For any $w\in S_{n}$ and $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , we define the following tilted relative positions:

$$ \displaystyle e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}gB \displaystyle\quad\text{if }gB\in X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}, \displaystyle w_{0}\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}gB \displaystyle\quad\text{if }gB\in\Omega^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}. $$

We now state several properties of classical and tilted relative positions.

#### Proposition 6.11.

Let $w\in S_{n}$ and $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ . Let $y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}\in\fl_{n}$ be flags. Then:

- (1) If $y_{1}\xrightarrow{w}y_{2}$ , then $y_{2}\xrightarrow{w^{-1}}y_{1}$ .

- (2) If $y_{1}\xrightarrow{w}y_{2}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y_{3}$ , then

$$ \begin{cases}y_{1}\xrightarrow{ws_{i}}y_{3}&\text{if }\ell(ws_{i})>\ell(w),\\ y_{1}\xrightarrow{ws_{i}}y_{3}\text{ or }y_{1}\xrightarrow{w}y_{3}&\text{if }\ell(ws_{i})<\ell(w).\end{cases} $$

- (3) If $e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y_{1}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y_{2}$ , then

$$ \begin{cases}e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}&\text{if }i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w),\\ e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}\text{ or }e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y_{2}&\text{if }i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w).\end{cases} $$

- (4) If $w_{0}\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y_{1}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y_{2}$ , then

$$ \begin{cases}w_{0}\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}&\text{if }i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w),\\ w_{0}\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}\text{ or }w_{0}\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y_{2}&\text{if }i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w).\end{cases} $$

- (5) Suppose $e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y$ . If $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ , then there exists a unique flag $y^{\prime}\in\fl_{n}$ such that

$$ e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y^{\prime}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y. $$

The map $\pi_{ws_{i}}^{w,\mathbf{a}}:X^{\circ}_{w,\mathbf{a}}\to X^{\circ}_{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}$ defined by $y\mapsto y^{\prime}$ is algebraic and given explicitly by

$$ gB\mapsto g\dot{s}_{i}B, $$

where $g\in G$ is the canonical representative of $gB$ , as described in Proposition 4.17.

#### Proof.

Parts (1) and (2) are stated in [43, Section 4.2]. For part (3), let $y_{1}=gB$ , where $g$ is the canonical representative of $gB$ as described in Proposition 4.17. Depending on whether $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ or $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ , the set of $\ast$ entries in the $i$ -th and $(i+1)$ -th columns of $g$ are nested. See Figure 14 for an illustration of the structure in these columns.

*(a) Case $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ .*

*(b) Case $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ .*

*Figure 14. The $i$ -th and $(i+1)$ -th row in the canonical representative described in Proposition 4.17. The red line indicates $a_{i}=a_{i+1}$ . Zero entries are omitted, and only nonzero entries are shown.*

Since $y_{1}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y_{2}$ , we have $y_{2}=g^{\prime}B$ , where $g^{\prime}=g\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}p&1\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ for some $p\in\mathbb{C}$ . We analyze the following cases:

- (1) If $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ (as in Figure 14(a)) and $p=0$ , then $e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}$ because $y_{2}=g^{\prime}B=g^{\prime}\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-c\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)B$ , and $g^{\prime}\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-c\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)=g\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ 1&-c\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is the canonical representative for $y_{2}\in X_{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

- (2) If $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ and $p\neq 0$ , then $e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y_{2}$ because $y_{2}=g^{\prime}B=g^{\prime}\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1/p&1\\ 0&-p\end{smallmatrix}\right)B$ , and $g^{\prime}\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1/p&1\\ 0&-p\end{smallmatrix}\right)=g\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 1/p&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is the canonical representative for $y_{2}\in X_{w,\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

- (3) If $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ (as in Figure 14(b)), then $e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y_{2}$ because $y_{2}=g^{\prime}B=g\cdot\phi_{i}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}p&1\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)B$ is already the canonical representative for $y_{2}\in X_{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ .

This completes the proof of (3). The argument for (4) is analogous. For part (5), existence follows from case (1): when $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w)$ and $p=0$ , we have $g\dot{s}_{i}B\in X_{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ . For uniqueness, suppose there exist two such flags $y^{\prime}$ and $y^{\prime\prime}$ . Then, by part (1), we have $y^{\prime}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y^{\prime\prime}$ , so by part (2), either $y^{\prime}=y^{\prime\prime}$ or $y^{\prime}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y^{\prime\prime}$ . In the latter case, since $e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y^{\prime}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}y^{\prime\prime}$ , applying part (3) yields $e\xrightarrow{w,\mathbf{a}}y^{\prime\prime}$ , which contradicts the assumption that $e\xrightarrow{ws_{i},\mathbf{a}}y^{\prime\prime}$ . ∎

We are now ready to define the tilted Deodhar cells. See Notation 6.1 for the notation used in the following proposition.

Now we are ready to state the main theorem of the tilted Deodhar decomposition.

#### Theorem 6.13.

Suppose $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , and let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ . Then the open tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}$ admits a decomposition into tilted Deodhar cells $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}$ , indexed by tilted distinguished subwords $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ corresponding to $u$ :

$$ \mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}},\quad\text{where }\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\cong(\mathbb{C}^{\ast})^{|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{\circ}|}\times\mathbb{C}^{|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}|}. $$

Each Deodhar cell $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}$ admits the following explicit parametrization:

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\cong\left\{gB=g_{1}g_{2}\cdots g_{\ell}B\;\middle|\;\begin{aligned} g_{j}&=\dot{s}_{i_{j}}&&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{u}}^{+},\\
g_{j}&=y_{i_{j}}(p_{j})&&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{u}}^{\circ},\\
g_{j}&=x_{\alpha_{i}}(m_{j})\dot{s}_{i_{j}}^{-1}&&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}.\end{aligned}\right\}, $$

where $p_{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{\ast}$ and $m_{j}\in\mathbb{C}$ are parameters.

It follows immediately from Proposition 6.12 that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is the disjoint union of tilted Deodhar cells $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}$ where $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ . It remains to prove the explicit parametrization.

We begin by introducing a definition needed for the argument. Define the standard chart $G_{u,\mathbf{a}}\subseteq G$ to be the set of matrices $M=(m_{i,k})_{i,k\in[n]}$ such that

$$ m_{i,k}=\begin{cases}\pm 1&\text{if }i=u_{k},\\
0&\text{if }i<_{a_{k}}u_{k}.\end{cases} $$
